title: Linux File Permissions and Ownership Deep Dive
summary: Go beyond rwx to master octal modes, ownership, the special bits, umask, and ACLs with confidence.
seo_title: Linux File Permissions and Ownership: A Practical Deep Dive
seo_description: Understand Linux permissions properly: read the rwx columns, use octal and symbolic chmod, set ownership, control umask, and apply setuid, setgid, the sticky bit, and ACLs.
seo_keywords: linux permissions, chmod, chown, octal, umask, setuid, setgid, sticky bit, getfacl, setfacl, ownership
sections: Permissions are a question about three audiences

Every file and directory on a Linux system answers the same question three times: what may the owner do, what may members of the file's group do, and what may everyone else do. The answer is stored as nine permission bits, three for each audience, and each trio offers the same three choices: read, write, and execute.

The reason this matters is that Linux is multi-user from the ground up. A web server process, a backup job, and a logged-in human can all touch the same filesystem at once, and the only thing standing between them is these bits. Learning to read them at a glance is the single most useful skill for keeping a system both functional and secure.

ls -l report.txt
# -rw-r--r-- 1 alice staff 482 Jun 18 09:14 report.txt
#  |\_/\_/\_/
#  |  |  |  \__ other: r-- (read only)
#  |  |  \_____ group: r-- (read only)
#  |  \________ owner: rw- (read + write)
#  \___________ file type: - means a regular file
bash
The first character is the type, not a permission: - file, d directory, l symlink.
What read, write, and execute actually mean

The three letters do not mean the same thing for files as they do for directories, and this trips up almost everyone at first. For a regular file, read lets you view its contents, write lets you change them, and execute lets you run it as a program or script.

For a directory the meanings shift. Read lets you list the names inside it, write lets you create, rename, or delete entries within it, and execute, often called the search bit, lets you enter the directory and reach files by name. A directory with read but not execute is nearly useless: you can see that names exist but cannot actually open anything inside.

# A directory you can list but not enter:
chmod 600 ~/locked_dir      # rw- for owner, no execute
ls ~/locked_dir             # may show names from the cached listing
cat ~/locked_dir/notes.txt  # Permission denied — no execute on the dir

# Restore the search bit:
chmod 700 ~/locked_dir      # rwx for owner
bash
Write on a directory controls deletion of files inside it, even files you do not own.
Octal mode: turning rwx into numbers

Symbolic permissions are easy to read but slow to type, so administrators lean on octal notation. Assign read the value 4, write the value 2, and execute the value 1, then add them up per audience. Read plus write is 6, read plus execute is 5, and all three is 7.

A full mode is three of these digits in owner-group-other order. So 644 means the owner has read and write while group and other get read only, and 755 means the owner has everything while group and other can read and execute but not modify. Once the addition becomes automatic you will read modes faster than the letters.

chmod 644 config.yaml   # rw-r--r--  typical for a data file
chmod 600 id_rsa        # rw-------  private key, owner only
chmod 755 deploy.sh     # rwxr-xr-x  runnable by anyone, editable by owner
chmod 775 shared/       # rwxrwxr-x  group can write into the directory

stat -c '%a %n' config.yaml id_rsa
# 644 config.yaml
# 600 id_rsa
bash
stat -c '%a' prints the octal mode directly, handy for scripts and double-checking.
Symbolic mode for surgical changes

Octal is great when you want to set an exact mode, but it is clumsy when you only want to toggle one bit. Symbolic mode lets you add, remove, or set permissions for a specific audience without disturbing the others. The audiences are u (user/owner), g (group), o (other), and a (all), combined with + to add, - to remove, and = to set exactly.

This is the safer choice when you are tweaking a file in place. Adding the execute bit to a script with chmod +x leaves its read and write bits untouched, whereas reaching for an octal value forces you to remember and restate everything.

chmod +x build.sh        # add execute for all audiences
chmod u+x,go-w build.sh  # owner can execute; remove write from group/other
chmod g=rx logs/         # group gets exactly read+execute, nothing else
chmod a-x archive.tar    # strip execute from everyone
chmod -R o-rwx private/  # recursively deny 'other' any access
bash
Combine clauses with commas; -R recurses, but be deliberate about applying file modes to directories.
Ownership: chown and chgrp

Permissions are only half the story; they decide what each audience may do, but ownership decides who falls into the owner and group audiences in the first place. Every file has exactly one owning user and one owning group. The chown command changes both, and chgrp changes just the group.

Changing ownership generally requires root, because handing a file to another user could be used to dodge quotas or smuggle setuid programs. A common real-world task is fixing a directory that was created by root but needs to belong to an application's service account so that account can write to it.

sudo chown alice report.txt           # change owner to alice
sudo chown alice:developers report.txt # change owner and group
sudo chgrp developers report.txt       # change only the group
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/app  # recursive, for a web app

ls -l report.txt
# -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 482 Jun 18 09:14 report.txt
bash
The colon syntax owner:group sets both at once; -R applies down a whole tree.
umask: the permissions you never see being set

You may have noticed that new files arrive as 644 and new directories as 755 without you ever running chmod. That default comes from the umask, a mask of bits to subtract from the system's base permissions (666 for files, 777 for directories). A umask of 022 removes write from group and other, which is why files land at 644.

Setting a tighter umask such as 077 means new files are private by default, readable and writable only by you. This is worth doing in scripts that create sensitive output, because it closes the gap where a file is briefly world-readable between creation and a later chmod.

umask                # show current mask, e.g. 0022
umask -S             # show it symbolically: u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx

umask 077            # new files now 600, new dirs 700
touch newfile && ls -l newfile
# -rw------- 1 alice alice 0 Jun 18 09:20 newfile

# Make it permanent for your shell by adding 'umask 077' to ~/.bashrc
bash
umask subtracts bits; it cannot add a permission the base mode never granted, such as execute on a plain file.
The special bits: setuid, setgid, and the sticky bit

Beyond the nine standard bits there are three special ones that change how execution and directory ownership behave. Setuid on an executable makes it run as the file's owner rather than the caller, which is how the unprivileged passwd command can edit the root-owned shadow file. Setgid does the same for the group, and on a directory it makes new files inherit that directory's group instead of the creator's primary group.

The sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion so that users can only remove their own files, even in a world-writable space. This is exactly why anyone can create files in /tmp but nobody can delete a neighbor's. In long listings these bits show up as s, S, or t in the execute positions.

chmod 4755 myprog     # leading 4 = setuid:  -rwsr-xr-x
chmod 2775 shared/    # leading 2 = setgid:  drwxrwsr-x (group inheritance)
chmod 1777 /tmp/scratch  # leading 1 = sticky: drwxrwxrwt

ls -ld /tmp
# drwxrwxrwt 18 root root 4096 Jun 18 09:25 /tmp  <- the trailing t
bash
An uppercase S or T means the special bit is set but the underlying execute bit is not — usually a mistake.
When three audiences are not enough: ACLs

The owner-group-other model is elegant but coarse. The moment you need to grant one extra user write access without changing the owning group, the classic bits run out of room. Access Control Lists (ACLs) extend the model with per-user and per-group entries layered on top of the standard permissions.

Use getfacl to inspect and setfacl to modify them. A files with extended ACLs shows a trailing + in ls -l. Default ACLs on a directory are especially powerful: every new file created inside automatically inherits the rules, which is the cleanest way to keep a shared project folder consistent without a nightly chmod cron job.

# Grant user 'bob' read+write on one file, leaving group/other alone:
setfacl -m u:bob:rw report.txt
getfacl report.txt
# user:bob:rw-

ls -l report.txt
# -rw-rw-r--+ 1 alice developers 482 Jun 18 report.txt   <- note the +

# Make every new file in a shared dir readable by the 'qa' group:
setfacl -d -m g:qa:r /srv/builds
setfacl -x u:bob report.txt   # remove bob's entry again
bash
-d sets a default (inherited) ACL on a directory; -x removes an entry; -b wipes all ACLs.
Practice it where you cannot break anything

Permissions are best learned by feel, and the only way to build that feel is to set a mode, run ls -l, predict what a command will do, and then watch it succeed or fail. Reading about the sticky bit teaches you the definition; trying to delete a neighbor's file in a 1777 directory teaches you what it is for.

Open the free in-browser Linux terminal, create a scratch directory, and walk through each section above: flip octal modes, change ownership, tighten your umask, set a setgid bit on a shared folder, and add an ACL for a fictional teammate. Nothing here needs a real server, and nothing you do can damage anything.

title: Managing Linux Processes and systemd Services
summary: See what is running, control it with signals and priorities, and run your own programs as managed systemd services.
seo_title: Linux Processes and systemd Services: A Hands-On Guide
seo_description: Inspect processes with ps and top, send signals, adjust priorities, and write a real systemd unit file with restart policies, logging via journalctl, and timers.
seo_keywords: linux processes, systemd, systemctl, journalctl, ps, top, signals, kill, unit file, service, timer, nice
sections: What a process actually is

A process is a running instance of a program: code loaded into memory, given its own address space, a process ID (PID), an owner, and a slice of CPU time. The kernel keeps a table of them all and schedules them onto the available cores. When you type a command in the shell, the shell forks a child process to run it and waits for it to finish.

Processes form a tree. Every process except the very first has a parent, recorded as its PPID. At the root sits PID 1, the init system, which on modern distributions is systemd. Understanding this hierarchy matters because killing a parent, orphaning children, and reparenting to PID 1 are everyday realities when something misbehaves.

ps -ef | head -5
# UID   PID  PPID  C STIME TTY      TIME     CMD
# root    1     0  0 08:00 ?        00:00:03 /sbin/init
# root  412     1  0 08:00 ?        00:00:00 /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-journald
# alice 980   975  0 08:01 pts/0    00:00:00 -bash
# alice 1042  980  0 08:02 pts/0    00:00:00 ps -ef
bash
PID 1 has PPID 0; notice how your shell and the ps command share a parent chain.
Listing processes with ps

The ps command takes a snapshot of processes at one instant. It has two competing flag styles for historical reasons, but two invocations cover almost everything. ps aux gives a wide, BSD-style view with CPU and memory percentages, while ps -ef gives the System V view that highlights the parent-child relationships.

In practice you rarely read the whole list; you pipe it through grep to find one program, or sort it to find the resource hogs. Learning to combine ps with grep, sort, and awk turns a wall of text into a precise answer to questions like which process is eating the most memory right now.

ps aux                       # every process, with %CPU and %MEM
ps aux | grep -i nginx       # find a specific program
ps -ef --forest              # show the parent/child tree visually

# Top five memory consumers:
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -6

# Just the PID of a named process (cleaner than grep):
pgrep -fl sshd
bash
pgrep avoids the classic 'grep finds its own grep' noise that plagues ps aux | grep.
Watching live with top and htop

ps is a still photograph; top is the live video. It refreshes every few seconds and sorts processes by CPU usage by default, making it the first tool you reach for when a machine feels sluggish. The header summarizes load average, memory, and swap, while the rows below update in place.

Inside top you can press keys to change behavior: M sorts by memory, P by CPU, and k prompts you to kill a PID. The load average shown is the number of processes wanting CPU averaged over one, five, and fifteen minutes; on a four-core box a load of 4.0 means fully busy, while 8.0 means twice as much work as the cores can handle.

top              # interactive; press q to quit, M for memory sort
top -b -n1 | head -12   # batch mode: one snapshot, scriptable

uptime
# 09:30:01 up 3 days,  2:14,  2 users,  load average: 0.41, 0.55, 0.60

# htop is a friendlier color version if installed:
htop
bash
Load average above your core count for sustained periods signals a CPU bottleneck.
Signals: how you talk to a process

You do not stop a process by force so much as politely ask it to. The kernel delivers signals — small numbered messages — and well-behaved programs install handlers to react to them. The kill command, despite its name, simply sends a signal of your choosing to a PID.

The two you use most are SIGTERM (15), the default, which says please shut down cleanly so the program can flush buffers and close files, and SIGKILL (9), which the kernel enforces immediately and the process cannot catch or ignore. Always try SIGTERM first; reach for SIGKILL only when a process is truly wedged, because killing it hard can leave half-written files behind.

kill 1042            # send SIGTERM (15) — the polite default
kill -TERM 1042      # the same thing, named explicitly
kill -HUP 412        # SIGHUP often tells a daemon to reload its config
kill -9 1042         # SIGKILL — last resort, cannot be caught

pkill -f 'python worker.py'   # kill by command pattern instead of PID
killall nginx                 # kill every process with that exact name
bash
SIGHUP is widely repurposed by daemons to mean 'reread your config file without restarting'.
Priorities: nice and renice

Not all work deserves equal CPU attention. The nice value, ranging from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest), nudges the scheduler about how generously to treat a process. A higher nice number means the process is nicer to its neighbors and yields CPU more readily, which is perfect for a background batch job you do not want to slow down an interactive session.

Launch a command with a chosen niceness using nice, or adjust a running process with renice. Lowering a niceness below zero requires root, because that lets a process demand more than its fair share. Niceness only affects CPU contention; if the system is idle, even a deprioritized job runs at full speed.

nice -n 10 ./long_import.sh    # start a job at low priority (nice 10)
renice -n 5 -p 1042            # make running PID 1042 nicer
sudo renice -n -5 -p 412       # raise priority (needs root)

ps -o pid,ni,comm -p 1042
#   PID  NI COMMAND
#  1042  10 long_import.sh
bash
Negative nice values prioritize a process and require root; positive values anyone can set.
Foreground, background, and jobs

A shell can manage several commands at once. Append an & to launch a command in the background so the prompt returns immediately, or press Ctrl+Z to suspend the current foreground job and drop back to the prompt. The jobs builtin lists what the shell is managing, and fg or bg resume a job in the foreground or background.

There is a catch: a backgrounded job is still tied to your shell, so closing the terminal sends it a hangup and usually kills it. For work that must survive a disconnect, prefix it with nohup, redirect its output to a file, or run it under a terminal multiplexer like tmux. For anything meant to run indefinitely on a server, a systemd service is the right answer — covered next.

long_task.sh &        # run in background; shell prints a job number
jobs                  # [1]+  Running    long_task.sh &
fg %1                 # bring job 1 to the foreground
# (press Ctrl+Z to suspend, then:)
bg %1                 # resume it in the background

nohup ./long_task.sh > out.log 2>&1 &   # survives terminal close
bash
& backgrounds within the shell; nohup detaches from the terminal's hangup signal.
systemd: the modern way to run services

Ad hoc background jobs are fine for experiments, but production work belongs to systemd, the init system that manages services (called units) on most Linux distributions. systemctl is the command you use to start, stop, enable, and inspect them. Enabling a unit means it starts automatically at boot; starting it means it runs right now.

The mental model is worth internalizing: start and stop control the current state, while enable and disable control the boot-time state, and the two are independent. A unit can be enabled but stopped, or running but not enabled. systemctl status ties it all together in one screen with the active state, the recent log lines, and the main PID.

systemctl status sshd          # running? enabled? recent logs?
sudo systemctl start nginx     # start it now
sudo systemctl stop nginx      # stop it now
sudo systemctl enable nginx    # start automatically at boot
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx  # enable AND start in one step
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
bash
enable/disable affect boot; start/stop affect now — they are deliberately separate controls.
Writing your own systemd unit file

The real power comes from running your own program as a managed service. A unit file is a small INI-style text file placed under /etc/systemd/system describing what to run and how to supervise it. The killer feature is Restart=on-failure: if your program crashes, systemd brings it back automatically, with backoff, no cron hacks required.

The file has three sections. [Unit] holds metadata and ordering (After=network.target says start me once networking is up). [Service] defines the command, the user it runs as, and the restart policy. [Install] tells systemd when to start it at boot. After writing or editing a unit you must run daemon-reload so systemd rereads it.

# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My background worker
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/myapp/worker.py
WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp
User=appuser
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
ini
Place under /etc/systemd/system, then: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
Reading logs with journalctl

systemd captures everything your service prints to standard output and standard error into a central journal, so you do not have to invent your own log file. journalctl queries that journal, and the -u flag scopes it to a single unit. This is usually the fastest path from a service won't stay up to the exact stack trace that explains why.

The flags you will use daily are -f to follow new lines live like tail -f, -e to jump to the end, --since to filter by time, and -p err to show only error-priority and above. Because the journal is structured and indexed, these filters are fast even on busy machines with weeks of history.

journalctl -u myapp.service          # all logs for one unit
journalctl -u myapp.service -f       # follow new entries live
journalctl -u myapp.service -e       # jump to the most recent lines
journalctl -u myapp.service --since '10 min ago'
journalctl -u myapp.service -p err   # errors and worse only
journalctl -b                        # everything since the last boot
bash
-u scopes to a unit, -f follows, --since accepts friendly times like 'yesterday' or '09:00'.
Scheduled jobs: systemd timers

Cron has run periodic jobs on Unix for decades, but systemd offers an integrated alternative: timers. A timer unit triggers a matching service unit on a schedule, and because the work runs as a normal service you get journald logging, dependency ordering, and missed-run catch-up for free.

You write two files that share a name: a .service that does the work and a .timer that says when. OnCalendar uses a clear syntax (daily, weekly, or an explicit time), and Persistent=true runs a job that was missed while the machine was off. Enable the .timer, not the .service, and systemd handles the rest.

# /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run the backup every day at 02:30

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# Enable it (pairs with backup.service):
# sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer
# systemctl list-timers   <- shows next run time
ini
Enable the .timer; it triggers backup.service. systemctl list-timers shows the schedule.
Put it together in the playground

You now have the full loop: find what is running, inspect and prioritize it, signal it correctly, and graduate from fragile background jobs to supervised systemd services with real logging and scheduling. Each idea is small on its own, but together they cover most of day-to-day Linux operations.

Open the free Linux terminal playground and rehearse the sequence end to end. List processes, send a SIGTERM and watch it land, renice a busy task, then write a tiny worker script and wrap it in a unit file with Restart=on-failure. Tail its journal, kill it, and watch systemd bring it back. That single exercise turns these commands from notes into instinct.

title: Linux Users, Groups, and sudo Explained
summary: Create and manage user accounts, organize access with groups, and grant precise privileges with sudo instead of sharing root.
seo_title: Linux Users, Groups, and sudo: A Practical Administration Guide
seo_description: Manage Linux accounts the right way: read /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, create users and groups, control password policy, and grant scoped privileges safely with sudo and the sudoers file.
seo_keywords: linux users, groups, sudo, useradd, usermod, passwd, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, sudoers, visudo, privilege
sections: Why accounts and groups exist

Linux assumes more than one entity uses a system, and not just humans: services, scheduled jobs, and containers all run as accounts too. Giving each its own identity means the kernel can enforce who owns which files, who may read a secret, and who may stop a service. The alternative — everyone sharing one all-powerful login — is how outages and breaches happen.

Groups add a second dimension. Rather than granting access to twenty people one at a time, you create a group, add the people to it, and grant the group. When someone joins or leaves the team you change one membership instead of hunting through every file. The whole users-and-groups system exists to make that kind of bulk, auditable access control possible.

id                       # show your own user, primary group, and extra groups
# uid=1000(alice) gid=1000(alice) groups=1000(alice),27(sudo),114(docker)

id alice                 # inspect any user
whoami                   # just the current username
groups                   # just the groups you belong to
bash
uid is your numeric user ID, gid your primary group; the groups list is your supplementary access.
Where account data actually lives

User and group definitions are plain text files, which makes Linux delightfully transparent. /etc/passwd holds one line per account: username, an x placeholder where the password used to sit, the numeric UID and GID, a comment field, the home directory, and the login shell. Despite the name it no longer stores passwords.

The actual hashed passwords live in /etc/shadow, readable only by root, which is what the x in passwd points to. Groups are listed in /etc/group, including each group's supplementary members. You should almost never edit these files by hand — the management commands keep them consistent — but knowing their layout lets you read a system at a glance.

getent passwd alice
# alice:x:1000:1000:Alice Smith:/home/alice:/bin/bash
#  |    |  |    |       |             |          \__ login shell
#  |    |  |    |       |             \_____________ home directory
#  |    |  |    |       \___________________________ comment / full name
#  |    |  |    \___________________________________ primary group GID
#  |    |  \________________________________________ user UID
#  |    \___________________________________________ password placeholder
#  \________________________________________________ username

sudo getent shadow alice    # hashed password + aging fields (root only)
getent group developers     # developers:x:1004:alice,bob,carol
bash
getent reads these databases including network sources like LDAP; prefer it over cat for portability.
Creating and removing users

useradd creates an account, but its defaults are spartan, so you almost always pass flags. The -m flag creates the home directory, -s sets the login shell, and -c records a comment such as the person's full name. A freshly created account has no password and cannot log in until you set one with passwd.

Deletion is the mirror image. userdel removes the account, and adding -r also deletes the home directory and mail spool. Be deliberate with -r: files owned by a removed user but living elsewhere become orphaned, showing only a numeric UID in listings, which is why offboarding usually means reassigning files before deleting the account.

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c 'Bob Jones' bob
sudo passwd bob              # set the initial password

sudo useradd -m -s /usr/sbin/nologin -c 'App service account' appsvc
# nologin gives a service account no interactive shell

sudo userdel -r bob         # remove bob and his home directory
find / -nouser 2>/dev/null  # hunt for files orphaned by deletions
bash
A login shell of /usr/sbin/nologin is the standard way to make a non-interactive service account.
Modifying accounts with usermod

Requirements change, and usermod edits an existing account without recreating it. You can rename the login with -l, change the shell with -s, move the home directory with -d (add -m to actually relocate the files), and lock or unlock the account with -L and -U.

The single most common usermod task is adding someone to a supplementary group. Here the -aG combination is critical: -G sets the supplementary group list, and the -a means append. Forgetting the -a replaces the entire list and silently removes the user from every other group, which is a classic way to lock yourself out of sudo. Group changes also only take effect in new login sessions.

sudo usermod -aG docker alice     # APPEND alice to the docker group
sudo usermod -aG sudo,developers bob   # add to several groups at once
sudo usermod -L bob               # lock the account (disable login)
sudo usermod -U bob               # unlock it again
sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh alice    # change the login shell

# Verify, then log out and back in for group changes to apply:
groups alice
bash
Always use -aG, never bare -G, or you will wipe the user's other group memberships.
Working with groups

Groups are created with groupadd, removed with groupdel, and renamed with groupmod. Every user has one primary group, recorded in /etc/passwd, which becomes the owning group of files they create. They can also belong to any number of supplementary groups listed in /etc/group, and those grant additional access.

The practical pattern for shared work is to create a project group, add the relevant users to it, and set the project directory to that group with the setgid bit so new files inherit it automatically. That combination — a group plus a setgid directory — is the canonical way several people collaborate in one folder without permission headaches.

sudo groupadd developers
sudo gpasswd -a alice developers    # add alice to the group
sudo gpasswd -d carol developers    # remove carol from the group

# Set up a shared, group-owned, inheriting directory:
sudo mkdir /srv/project
sudo chgrp developers /srv/project
sudo chmod 2775 /srv/project        # 2 = setgid: new files inherit the group

newgrp developers   # switch your active primary group for this shell
bash
The setgid bit (the leading 2 in 2775) makes every new file in the directory inherit the group.
Password and account aging policy

Setting a password is only the start; the chage command controls its lifecycle. You can force expiry after a number of days, require a minimum interval between changes, warn users before a password expires, and set an absolute date after which the account is disabled entirely — useful for contractors with a known end date.

These aging fields live in /etc/shadow and are easy to forget exist. A common task is forcing a freshly created user to choose their own password at first login by expiring it immediately, so the temporary password you set never becomes a permanent shared secret. chage -l prints the current settings in a readable form.

sudo chage -l bob                  # list bob's aging settings
sudo chage -d 0 bob                # expire now: force a change at next login
sudo chage -M 90 -W 7 bob          # max age 90 days, warn 7 days before
sudo chage -E 2026-12-31 bob       # disable the account after this date

passwd -S bob                      # status: P = usable, L = locked, NP = none
bash
chage -d 0 is the standard trick to force a password reset at the user's next login.
sudo: borrowing privilege, not sharing root

Logging in as root directly is dangerous: there is no record of who did what, and a single mistake runs with unlimited power. sudo solves this by letting named users run specific commands as root (or another user) using their own password, with every invocation logged. The principle is least privilege — grant the smallest capability that gets the job done.

Membership in a single group usually confers broad sudo rights: sudo on Debian and Ubuntu, wheel on Red Hat family systems. Adding a user to that group is the quick path to full administrative access. But sudo can be far more precise than all-or-nothing, which is the whole point of the sudoers file covered next.

sudo whoami              # prints 'root' — you ran it as root
sudo -l                  # list exactly what you are allowed to run
sudo -u appsvc whoami    # run a command as a different non-root user
sudo -i                  # start an interactive root shell (use sparingly)

# Grant broad admin access by group membership:
sudo usermod -aG sudo bob        # Debian/Ubuntu
# sudo usermod -aG wheel bob     # RHEL/Fedora/CentOS
bash
sudo -l is invaluable: it tells you precisely which commands your account may run elevated.
Editing sudoers safely with visudo

The rules that govern sudo live in /etc/sudoers and files under /etc/sudoers.d. Never open these with a plain editor: a single syntax error can lock everyone out of sudo at once. Always use visudo, which validates the file on save and refuses to install a broken version, and prefer dropping a small file into /etc/sudoers.d over editing the main file.

A rule reads as user host = (run-as) commands. You can scope a user to exactly one command — letting a deploy account restart one service and nothing else — and the NOPASSWD tag skips the password prompt for automation. Aliases let you name sets of commands or hosts to keep large policies readable.

# Run this, never edit the file directly:
sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy

# Let 'deploy' restart only nginx, without a password prompt:
deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx

# Give 'bob' full admin on every host:
bob ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL

# Let the 'webops' group manage web services as the www-data user:
%webops ALL=(www-data) /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp
bash
visudo syntax-checks before saving; a % prefix means the rule applies to a group, not a user.
Audit, then practice

Good account hygiene is mostly about being able to answer questions on demand: who can become root, which accounts can still log in, and who belongs to a sensitive group. A few commands answer all of these, and running them periodically is how you catch the stale contractor account or the over-broad sudo rule before someone else does.

Now build the muscle memory in the free Linux playground. Create a couple of users, organize them into a group, set up a setgid shared directory, expire a password to force a reset, and write a tightly scoped sudoers rule with visudo. Then run sudo -l as that user and confirm it can do exactly one thing and no more. That is least privilege you can see working.

# Everyone who can use sudo via group membership:
getent group sudo wheel 2>/dev/null

# Accounts with a real login shell (potential interactive users):
getent passwd | awk -F: '$7 ~ /(bash|zsh|sh)$/ {print $1}'

# Accounts with no password set (cannot log in by password):
sudo awk -F: '($2 == "" || $2 == "!") {print $1}' /etc/shadow
bash
Run these as a quick recurring audit to catch stale accounts and over-broad privileges.

title: Linux Disks, LVM, and Filesystems in Practice
summary: Understand block devices, partition disks, build flexible storage with LVM, create filesystems, and mount them persistently.
seo_title: Linux Disks, LVM, and Filesystems: A Hands-On Storage Guide
seo_description: Master Linux storage end to end: inspect block devices, partition disks, build physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes with LVM, make filesystems, mount via /etc/fstab, and grow volumes online.
seo_keywords: linux storage, lvm, lsblk, fdisk, parted, mkfs, mount, fstab, pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, lvextend, resize2fs, ext4, xfs
sections: The storage stack from device to directory

Linux storage is a layered stack, and most confusion comes from not knowing which layer you are working at. At the bottom sit block devices: whole disks like /dev/sda and their partitions like /dev/sda1. On top of a block device you create a filesystem, the structure that turns raw blocks into files and directories. Finally you mount that filesystem at a directory so its contents appear in the unified tree.

LVM, the Logical Volume Manager, inserts a flexible middle layer between partitions and filesystems. Instead of formatting a partition directly, you pool one or more devices and carve logical volumes out of the pool, which you can then grow, shrink, and move without repartitioning. The rest of this tutorial walks up the stack, then through LVM, then back down to a mounted, persistent filesystem.

lsblk
# NAME   MAJ:MIN RM  SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
# sda      8:0    0  100G  0 disk
# ├─sda1   8:1    0    1G  0 part /boot
# └─sda2   8:2    0   99G  0 part
#   ├─vg0-root 253:0 0 40G 0 lvm  /
#   └─vg0-data 253:1 0 30G 0 lvm  /data
# sdb      8:16   0   50G  0 disk
bash
lsblk is the map of the whole stack: disks, partitions, LVM volumes, and where each is mounted.
Inspecting block devices

Before changing anything, learn to read what is already there, because storage mistakes are unforgiving. lsblk is the friendliest view, showing the tree of disks, partitions, and LVM volumes with sizes and mount points. blkid reports each device's filesystem type and UUID, which you will need when mounting. df shows usage from the filesystem's point of view, while lsblk and friends show the device side.

A frequent source of error is confusing a device that is full of blocks with a filesystem that is full of data, or mixing up which /dev node corresponds to which physical disk. Cross-checking lsblk, blkid, and df against each other before you partition or format anything is cheap insurance against wiping the wrong device.

lsblk -f                 # tree view including filesystem type and UUID
blkid /dev/sda1          # /dev/sda1: UUID="..." TYPE="ext4"
df -hT                   # filesystem usage, human-readable, with type
sudo fdisk -l /dev/sda   # detailed partition table for one disk

# Total size vs. inode usage (running out of either fills a disk):
df -h /data
df -i /data
bash
df -h reports space; df -i reports inodes. A disk can be full of either even when the other looks fine.
Partitioning a disk

A new disk usually needs a partition table before use. Modern systems use GPT (the GUID Partition Table), which supports large disks and many partitions; the older MBR scheme is limited to 2 TB and four primary partitions. Two tools dominate: parted is scriptable and GPT-friendly, while fdisk is the classic interactive editor that now handles GPT too.

Partitioning is destructive in the sense that it rewrites the table the system uses to find data, so always confirm you are operating on the right device, ideally a fresh or scratch disk like /dev/sdb. After creating partitions, run partprobe or re-read the table so the kernel learns about the new /dev/sdbN nodes before you try to format them.

# Non-interactive with parted: a GPT label and one full-disk partition
sudo parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
sudo parted -s /dev/sdb mkpart primary 0% 100%

# Mark it for LVM use (sets the LVM partition type flag):
sudo parted -s /dev/sdb set 1 lvm on

sudo partprobe /dev/sdb     # make the kernel re-read the table
lsblk /dev/sdb              # confirm sdb1 now exists
bash
Double-check the device name; parted -s runs without prompting, so there is no second chance.
LVM, layer one: physical volumes

LVM has three layers stacked on top of your partitions. The lowest is the physical volume (PV), which is simply a partition or whole disk that you have initialized for LVM use with pvcreate. This writes a small header that lets LVM recognize and manage the device; it does not erase data elsewhere on the system, but it does claim that device.

Think of a PV as a raw building block of capacity. You can have many of them, spread across several disks. The flexibility of LVM begins here: because the filesystem will later sit on a logical volume rather than directly on this partition, you are free to add more PVs to the pool over time as storage needs grow.

sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1
# Physical volume "/dev/sdb1" successfully created.

sudo pvs                 # concise list of physical volumes
#   PV         VG   Fmt  Attr PSize  PFree
#   /dev/sdb1       lvm2 ---  50.00g 50.00g

sudo pvdisplay /dev/sdb1   # full detail for one PV
bash
pvs gives a one-line summary; pvdisplay gives the verbose view. A fresh PV has no volume group yet.
LVM, layer two: volume groups

Physical volumes on their own are just labeled capacity. The volume group (VG) is the pool that combines one or more PVs into a single addressable space, measured in fixed chunks called extents (4 MB by default). Once PVs join a VG, the system stops caring which physical disk a given chunk lives on — the VG is one big bucket of extents.

This pooling is what makes LVM powerful. Need more room in the group later? Run pvcreate on another disk and vgextend the group onto it, and the new capacity is instantly available to carve into volumes, with no downtime and no repartitioning of existing data. vgs shows how much of the pool is free to allocate.

sudo vgcreate data_vg /dev/sdb1
# Volume group "data_vg" successfully created

sudo vgs
#   VG       #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize  VFree
#   data_vg    1   0   0 wz--n- 50.00g 50.00g

# Later, grow the pool by adding another disk:
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc1
sudo vgextend data_vg /dev/sdc1     # capacity instantly available
bash
vgextend adds a disk's capacity to the pool live; the volume group abstracts away which disk holds what.
LVM, layer three: logical volumes

The logical volume (LV) is what you actually use: a slice of the volume group that behaves like a partition and gets a device node such as /dev/data_vg/app. You size it with lvcreate, either by an absolute size with -L or by a percentage of free space with -l. Unlike a real partition, an LV's boundaries are logical, which is exactly why it can be resized later.

You can create several LVs from one VG — say one for application data and one for database files — and each can grow independently as long as the pool has free extents. This is the everyday payoff of LVM: capacity planning becomes a runtime decision rather than something you must get perfect at install time.

sudo lvcreate -L 20G -n app data_vg       # a 20 GiB LV named 'app'
sudo lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n logs data_vg # use all remaining space

sudo lvs
#   LV   VG       Attr       LSize  ...
#   app  data_vg  -wi-a----- 20.00g
#   logs data_vg  -wi-a----- 30.00g

ls -l /dev/data_vg/        # device nodes for each LV
bash
-L sets an absolute size, -l takes extents or a percentage like 100%FREE; -n names the volume.
Creating a filesystem

A logical volume is still just blocks until you put a filesystem on it. mkfs writes the structures that track files, directories, free space, and metadata. The two dominant choices on Linux are ext4, the mature general-purpose default, and xfs, which excels with large files and high parallelism and is the default on Red Hat systems. Both are journaling filesystems, meaning they log metadata changes so a crash leaves the structure consistent.

Formatting is destructive to anything previously on the volume, so confirm the target device one more time. After formatting, note that ext4 can be both grown and shrunk, while xfs can only be grown — a real consideration if you ever expect to reclaim space, and the reason ext4 is often chosen for volumes that may need to shrink.

sudo mkfs.ext4 -L appdata /dev/data_vg/app
# Creating filesystem with ... 4k blocks ... done

# Or XFS, common on RHEL-family systems:
sudo mkfs.xfs -L logs /dev/data_vg/logs

sudo blkid /dev/data_vg/app    # confirm TYPE and grab the UUID
bash
ext4 can grow and shrink; xfs can only grow. Choose accordingly if reclaiming space matters.
Mounting and making it persistent with fstab

A filesystem must be mounted onto a directory to be usable. mount attaches it immediately, but a manual mount vanishes on reboot. For permanence you add an entry to /etc/fstab, the table the system consults at boot. Reference the filesystem by its UUID rather than the /dev path, because device names like /dev/sdb can change when disks are added or reordered, whereas a UUID is stable.

The golden rule of fstab edits is to test before you trust. A bad entry can stop the machine from booting. After editing, run mount -a to mount everything in the file right now; if it succeeds without error, the entry is safe and reboots will work. systemd users can also run systemctl daemon-reload so the unit generators pick up the change.

sudo mkdir -p /srv/app
UUID=$(sudo blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/data_vg/app)

# Add a line to /etc/fstab (shown here; edit the file to add it):
# UUID=<uuid>  /srv/app  ext4  defaults  0 2
echo "UUID=$UUID  /srv/app  ext4  defaults  0 2" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

sudo mount -a              # mount everything in fstab now — TEST it
df -hT /srv/app            # confirm it mounted as ext4
bash
Always run mount -a after editing fstab; a typo here can block the next boot. Reference by UUID, not /dev path.
Growing storage online

The reason you went through all those LVM layers is this moment: extending a volume without downtime. The procedure is two steps and order matters. First grow the logical volume with lvextend so it claims more extents from the pool, then grow the filesystem on top so it uses the new space. Doing only the first leaves the extra capacity invisible to applications.

The filesystem-growth command differs by type: resize2fs for ext4 and xfs_growfs for xfs, and the xfs version takes the mount point rather than the device. The handy lvextend -r flag does both steps at once. All of this works on a mounted, live filesystem, which is the entire promise of LVM made concrete.

# Grow the LV by 10 GiB, taken from free extents in the VG:
sudo lvextend -L +10G /dev/data_vg/app

# Then grow the filesystem to fill the larger LV:
sudo resize2fs /dev/data_vg/app          # ext4
# sudo xfs_growfs /srv/app               # xfs: pass the MOUNT POINT

# Or do both in one command with -r (resize filesystem):
sudo lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/data_vg/app

df -hT /srv/app          # confirm the new, larger size
bash
Extend the LV first, then the filesystem. lvextend -r does both at once and works while mounted.
When things go wrong: checking and repairing

Filesystems can develop inconsistencies after a crash, a bad disk, or a power loss, and Linux gives you tools to verify and repair them. fsck checks and fixes ext-family filesystems, but it must run on an unmounted filesystem, so you either unmount it first or schedule the check for the next boot. Running fsck on a mounted, live filesystem can corrupt it, so the tools refuse by default — respect that.

For xfs the equivalents are xfs_repair, also run unmounted. Beyond repair, monitoring matters: keep an eye on free space and inodes with df, watch for read-only remounts (a kernel safety reaction to errors) in the journal, and check SMART data on physical disks. Most catastrophic data loss is preceded by warnings nobody was watching for.

sudo umount /srv/app             # must be unmounted first
sudo fsck -f /dev/data_vg/app    # force a full ext4 check
sudo mount /srv/app              # remount when clean

# XFS uses its own repair tool (also unmounted):
# sudo xfs_repair /dev/data_vg/logs

# Watch the journal for read-only remounts signaling FS errors:
journalctl -k | grep -i 'remount\|ext4-fs error\|I/O error'
bash
Never fsck a mounted filesystem. Unmount first, or schedule the check for the next boot.
Rehearse the full stack safely

Storage is the area where a single mistyped device name does irreversible damage, which makes a throwaway practice environment uniquely valuable — it is the one place you can wipe a disk on purpose and learn from it with zero consequences. The skills compound: every concept here, from lsblk to lvextend, builds on the layer below it.

Open the free Linux playground and walk the whole stack on a scratch device: inspect it with lsblk, partition it, build a PV, VG, and LV, format ext4, mount it through fstab and verify with mount -a, then extend the LV and grow the filesystem online. Finish by unmounting and running fsck. Do that once end to end and the layered model of Linux storage will click into place for good.

title: Docker Images and Dockerfiles: Build Your Own
summary: Understand what a Docker image really is and write Dockerfiles that build small, repeatable images.
seo_title: Docker Images and Dockerfiles Explained — Build Your First Image
seo_description: Learn what a Docker image is, how layers and the build cache work, and how to write a clean Dockerfile. Practise live in a free Docker playground.
seo_keywords: docker image, dockerfile, build image, docker layers, build cache, tags, containerisation, beginner
sections: What an image actually is

When people say "Docker image" they often picture a single mysterious file. It is more useful to think of an image as a stack of read-only layers plus a small JSON manifest that records how to start a program. Each layer is a set of filesystem changes — files added, modified, or deleted — and the layers sit on top of one another like sheets of tracing paper. The final image is what you see when you look down through all of them.

Because layers are immutable and content-addressed, two images that share a base layer literally reuse the same bytes on disk. That is why pulling a second image based on the same Ubuntu release is so fast: most of it is already there. Holding this mental model now will make everything else about Docker feel less magical.

docker pull alpine:3.20
docker image inspect alpine:3.20 --format '{{.RootFS.Layers}}'
docker history alpine:3.20
bash
docker history shows the layers and the command that produced each one.
Image names and tags

An image reference has three parts: an optional registry, a repository name, and a tag. In `docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim`, the registry is Docker Hub, the repository is `library/python`, and the tag is `3.12-slim`. When you omit the registry Docker assumes Docker Hub, and when you omit the tag it assumes `latest` — which is just a conventional name, not a promise that the image is the newest.

Get into the habit of pinning a real tag rather than relying on `latest`. A build that says `python:3.12-slim` will behave the same way next month; one that says `python` might silently jump a major version and break your code. Tags are cheap, so use them deliberately.

docker pull python:3.12-slim
docker tag python:3.12-slim myteam/api:dev
docker images | grep -E 'python|api'
bash
docker tag just adds a second name to the same image — no copy is made.
Your first Dockerfile

A Dockerfile is a plain text recipe. Docker reads it top to bottom and turns most instructions into a new layer. The four you will use constantly are `FROM` (choose a base image), `COPY` (bring files in from your project), `RUN` (execute a command at build time), and `CMD` (the default command when a container starts).

The example below packages a tiny Python web app. Notice that `FROM` comes first — every image is built on top of another image, all the way down to a minimal base. The `WORKDIR` instruction sets the directory that later instructions and the running container use, so you do not have to repeat long paths.

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
dockerfile
Save this as 'Dockerfile' (no extension) in your project root.
Building and running it

The `docker build` command turns a Dockerfile into an image. The `-t` flag tags it with a name you choose, and the final `.` tells Docker the build context — the folder whose contents are available to `COPY`. Everything in that folder is sent to the builder, so keep it tidy.

Once built, the image is just like any image you pulled from a registry: you run it with `docker run`. If your app listens on a port, publish it with `-p host:container` so you can reach it from your browser.

docker build -t myteam/api:dev .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 myteam/api:dev
bash
--rm deletes the container when it exits so stopped containers do not pile up.
Why instruction order matters: the build cache

Docker caches each layer and reuses it on the next build if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. The instant one layer changes, every layer after it is rebuilt. This single rule explains the most important Dockerfile habit: copy the things that rarely change before the things that change constantly.

In the first Dockerfile we copied `requirements.txt` and ran `pip install` before copying the rest of the source. That ordering is deliberate. When you edit your application code, the dependency layer is still valid, so Docker skips the slow `pip install` and your rebuild takes a second instead of a minute. Reverse the order and every code edit reinstalls every dependency.

# Slow: any code change busts the dependency cache
COPY . .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Fast: dependencies cached separately from source
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
dockerfile
Order your COPY and RUN steps from least- to most-frequently-changed.
Keeping junk out with .dockerignore

Because the whole build context is sent to the builder and `COPY . .` grabs everything, an unguarded build can sweep in your `.git` history, local virtual environments, and editor files. That bloats the image, slows the build, and risks leaking secrets. A `.dockerignore` file fixes this — it works just like `.gitignore` and is read automatically.

List anything that should never end up in an image: dependency caches you reinstall during the build, build artefacts, and local configuration. A good `.dockerignore` is one of the cheapest ways to make an image smaller and a build faster.

# .dockerignore
.git
.gitignore
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
node_modules/
.env
Dockerfile
bash
Place this beside your Dockerfile; Docker applies it during build.
Inspecting and cleaning up

As you experiment you will accumulate images, including unnamed "dangling" ones left behind when a tag moves to a freshly built image. A few commands keep things under control. `docker images` lists what you have, `docker image inspect` dumps the full metadata, and `docker image prune` reclaims space.

Be deliberate about pruning. The plain `prune` removes only dangling images, which is safe. Adding `-a` removes every image not currently used by a container, which is aggressive — handy on a build server, surprising on your laptop when your next build has to re-pull everything.

docker images
docker image prune          # remove dangling (untagged) images
docker image prune -a       # remove ALL unused images — use with care
bash
Run plain prune often; reserve -a for when you genuinely want a clean slate.
Where to go next

You can now describe what an image is, read and write a basic Dockerfile, and explain why instruction order changes how fast your builds run. That is the foundation everything else in Docker stands on.

The fastest way to lock it in is to build something yourself. Open the free Docker playground, create the small Dockerfile above, change one line of source, and rebuild — watch which layers come from the cache and which get rebuilt. Once that clicks, you are ready to move on to running and connecting containers.

title: Docker Containers, Volumes, and Networks
summary: Run and manage containers, persist data with volumes, and let containers talk to each other over a network.
seo_title: Docker Containers, Volumes, and Networks — A Practical Guide
seo_description: Manage the container lifecycle, keep data with named volumes, and connect containers on user-defined networks. Hands-on examples in a free Docker playground.
seo_keywords: docker container, docker volume, docker network, persist data, container lifecycle, bridge network, docker exec
sections: The container lifecycle

A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image, and it moves through a small set of states: created, running, paused, stopped, and finally removed. Understanding these states clears up a lot of early confusion — for example, why `docker ps` shows nothing after a container exits even though the container still exists.

The key insight is that stopping a container does not delete it. Its writable layer and metadata stick around until you remove it, which is why `docker ps -a` can fill up with the ghosts of past experiments. Knowing the lifecycle lets you reason about where your data lives and when it disappears.

docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27       # create + start, detached
docker stop web                             # graceful stop
docker start web                            # bring it back
docker ps -a                                # see it in any state
docker rm -f web                            # stop and remove
bash
Name your containers with --name so you are not juggling random IDs.
Looking inside a running container

When something misbehaves you rarely rebuild — you investigate. `docker logs` shows whatever the main process wrote to standard output and error, which is where most applications send their diagnostics. `docker exec` runs an extra command inside an already-running container, most often an interactive shell so you can poke around.

The `-it` flags on `exec` are worth memorising: `-i` keeps input open and `-t` allocates a terminal, and together they give you a usable interactive prompt. Remember that anything you change this way lives only in that container's writable layer and vanishes when the container is removed.

docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27
docker logs web                  # view stdout/stderr
docker logs -f web               # follow new output live
docker exec -it web sh           # open a shell inside the container
bash
Type 'exit' to leave the exec shell; the container keeps running.
Why container data is ephemeral

Every container gets a thin writable layer stacked on top of its read-only image layers. Files an application creates at runtime — a database's data directory, uploaded user files — land in that writable layer. The catch is that the writable layer is bound to the container's life: remove the container and the layer goes with it.

You can prove this to yourself. Write a file inside a container, remove the container, start a fresh one from the same image, and the file is gone. This is by design — containers are meant to be disposable — but it means any data you care about must be stored outside the container. That is exactly what volumes are for.

docker run --name tmp alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo hi > /data.txt'
docker rm tmp
docker run --name tmp alpine:3.20 cat /data.txt   # error: file is gone
bash
The second run starts a brand-new container — the previous writable layer is gone.
Named volumes: data that outlives containers

A volume is storage that Docker manages outside any single container's writable layer. Mount the same named volume into a new container and the data is right where you left it. This decoupling is what lets you upgrade an image — say from one database version to the next — without losing the data, because the data was never inside the container in the first place.

The `-v name:/path` syntax mounts a named volume at a path inside the container. Docker creates the volume on first use. Below, a PostgreSQL container stores its data in a volume named `pgdata`; destroy and recreate the container as often as you like and the database survives.

docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16

docker rm -f db        # remove the container...
# ...recreate it with the same volume and the data is still there
docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
bash
Named volumes are managed by Docker; list them with 'docker volume ls'.
Bind mounts for live development

A volume is the right tool for application data, but during development you often want a container to see files on your host as you edit them. A bind mount maps a host directory straight into the container, so saving a file in your editor is instantly visible inside the running container — perfect for code with live reload.

The distinction is worth holding onto: named volumes are managed by Docker and ideal for data you want to persist and move between containers; bind mounts point at a specific host path and are ideal for development and for injecting config. Use an absolute host path (`$(pwd)` resolves the current directory) so there is no ambiguity about what is being mounted.

docker run -d --name site \
  -p 8080:80 \
  -v "$(pwd)/public:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro" \
  nginx:1.27
bash
The :ro suffix mounts the host folder read-only inside the container.
Containers on a network

Containers on the default bridge network are isolated from each other by name, which is why early experiments often resort to fragile IP addresses. Create your own user-defined bridge network instead and Docker gives you automatic DNS: every container can reach the others by their container name. This is the foundation of any multi-service setup.

In the example, an app container and a Redis container join the network `appnet`. From inside the app container you connect to the host named `cache` — no IP addresses, no configuration files to update when something restarts. The name is stable for as long as the container exists on the network.

docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name cache --network appnet redis:7
docker run -d --name app --network appnet -p 3000:3000 myteam/app:dev

# inside 'app', this resolves to the redis container:
docker exec -it app sh -c 'getent hosts cache'
bash
User-defined networks give you name-based DNS between containers for free.
Publishing ports versus internal traffic

There are two different kinds of connectivity and mixing them up causes a lot of head-scratching. Traffic between containers on the same user-defined network flows freely using container names and the container's own ports — you do not publish anything for that. Publishing with `-p` is only about reaching a container from the host or the outside world.

A common pattern makes this concrete: publish the web frontend so users can reach it, but leave the database unpublished. The app talks to the database over the shared network by name, while the database stays unreachable from outside the host. Fewer published ports means a smaller attack surface, so publish only what truly needs to face the world.

docker network create appnet
# Database: reachable by other containers, NOT published to the host
docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16
# Web app: published so a browser can reach it on localhost:8000
docker run -d --name web --network appnet -p 8000:8000 myteam/web:dev
bash
Only 'web' is reachable from your host; 'db' is reachable only by 'web'.
Cleaning up the moving parts

Containers, volumes, and networks each accumulate, and each has its own prune command so you can clean up precisely. Stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images go with `docker system prune`. Volumes are deliberately excluded from that command because they usually hold data you want to keep — you must opt in explicitly.

Treat volume pruning with the same caution as deleting a database. Run `docker volume ls` first, confirm nothing important is unattached, and only then prune. The rest of the cleanup is low-risk and worth doing regularly to reclaim disk space.

docker container prune       # remove all stopped containers
docker network prune          # remove unused user-defined networks
docker volume ls              # ALWAYS review before removing volumes
docker system prune           # containers + networks + dangling images (NOT volumes)
bash
system prune leaves volumes alone on purpose — your data is safe by default.
Where to go next

You can now run containers through their full lifecycle, keep data alive with volumes, develop against bind mounts, and wire containers together on a private network. These are the building blocks of every real application running in containers.

Managing several `docker run` commands by hand quickly gets tedious, though — and that is the cue for the next step. Try these examples in the free Docker playground first, then move on to Docker Compose, which lets you declare this whole arrangement of containers, volumes, and networks in a single file.

title: Docker Compose: Multi-Service Applications
summary: Define a whole multi-container app — services, volumes, and networks — in one Compose file and run it with a single command.
seo_title: Docker Compose Tutorial — Multi-Service Apps in One File
seo_description: Use Docker Compose to declare services, volumes, networks, dependencies, and health checks for a multi-container app. Hands-on in a free Docker playground.
seo_keywords: docker compose, compose file, multi-service, depends_on, healthcheck, docker compose up, environment variables, profiles
sections: From many docker run commands to one file

Once an application has a web tier, a database, and a cache, running it by hand means a stack of `docker run` commands plus a network and a volume to create first — and remembering the exact flags every time. Docker Compose replaces all of that with a single declarative file that describes the desired end state. You run `docker compose up` and Compose creates the networks, volumes, and containers for you in the right order.

Think of Compose as infrastructure-as-code for a single host. The file is the source of truth: anyone who checks out your project gets the same stack, and tearing it all down is one command. Note that modern Docker ships Compose as a subcommand — `docker compose` (with a space), not the older standalone `docker-compose`.

docker compose version
docker compose up -d      # start everything in the background
docker compose ps         # see the services and their state
docker compose down       # stop and remove containers + networks
bash
Run these from the directory containing your compose.yaml.
Anatomy of a compose file

A Compose file is YAML with a top-level `services` map; each key under it is one service, which becomes one container. A service either points at an existing image with `image:` or builds one from a Dockerfile with `build:`. Around the services you can declare named `volumes:` and `networks:` that the services reference.

The file below describes a two-service app: a web service built from the local Dockerfile and a Postgres database using an official image. Compose automatically creates a default network and attaches every service to it, so `web` can reach `db` by the service name `db` — the same name-based DNS you set up manually with `docker network create`, now handled for you.

services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
yaml
Save as compose.yaml; 'web' reaches the database at host 'db'.
Startup order with depends_on and health checks

Services often need each other in a particular order — the web app should not accept traffic before the database is ready. `depends_on` controls the order in which Compose starts containers, but on its own it only waits for the container to *start*, not for the program inside to be *ready*. A Postgres container can be running for several seconds before it actually accepts connections.

The robust pattern is a health check combined with `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`. Compose then waits until the database reports healthy before starting the web service. This eliminates the classic flaky-startup race where the app crashes on boot because the database was not listening yet.

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
  web:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
yaml
web now waits until the db health check passes before starting.
Configuration with environment variables and .env

Hard-coding passwords and connection strings in the Compose file is a habit worth breaking early. Compose automatically reads a file named `.env` in the project directory and substitutes `${VAR}` placeholders, so secrets and per-environment values live outside the file you commit. Add `.env` to your `.gitignore` and commit a `.env.example` with blank values as documentation.

There are two distinct uses of variables, and keeping them straight avoids confusion. Substitution like `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` is resolved by Compose while reading the YAML. The `environment:` block, by contrast, sets variables *inside* the running container for the application to read. The example below uses both.

# .env  (do not commit this)
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=super-secret
WEB_PORT=8000

# compose.yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "${WEB_PORT}:8000"
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
yaml
Compose substitutes ${...} from .env when it parses the file.
Working with a running stack

Day-to-day you interact with the whole stack through `docker compose`, which targets services by name rather than container ID. `logs` aggregates output from one or all services, `exec` opens a shell or runs a command inside a service, and `up --build` rebuilds images before starting when you have changed a Dockerfile.

A detail that saves a lot of frustration: editing the Compose file or a Dockerfile does not change anything until you re-run `up`. Compose compares the desired state in the file against what is running and recreates only the services that changed, leaving the rest untouched. So the loop is edit, then `docker compose up -d`, and Compose figures out the minimal set of changes.

docker compose up -d --build      # rebuild changed images, then start
docker compose logs -f web        # follow one service's logs
docker compose exec web sh        # shell into the web service
docker compose restart web        # restart a single service
bash
Compose recreates only the services whose config or image changed.
Scaling and optional services with profiles

Two features turn Compose from a toy into something genuinely useful. Scaling runs multiple replicas of a stateless service with `--scale`; because each replica joins the same network under the same service name, requests are spread across them — handy for load testing a worker tier. Stateful services like databases should not be scaled this way.

Profiles let you mark services as optional so they only start when you ask for them. A `tools` profile might hold a database admin UI or a one-off migration runner that you do not want running all the time. Services without a profile always start; services in a profile start only when that profile is activated.

# compose.yaml — pgadmin only starts when the 'tools' profile is on
services:
  worker:
    build: .
  pgadmin:
    image: dpage/pgadmin4
    profiles: ["tools"]

# run 3 workers; pgadmin stays off
docker compose up -d --scale worker=3
# now bring up the optional tooling
docker compose --profile tools up -d
bash
Scale stateless services only; keep databases at a single replica.
Overrides for dev versus production

The same application usually needs different settings in development and production — bind-mounted source and debug logging locally, baked-in images and restart policies in production. Rather than maintaining two divergent files, keep a base `compose.yaml` and layer changes on top with override files passed via `-f`. Files listed later win, merging into the earlier ones.

Compose even reads `compose.override.yaml` automatically when present, which is the conventional home for local-only tweaks. The discipline here is to keep the base file production-shaped and put developer conveniences — bind mounts, exposed debug ports, looser settings — in the override, so production never accidentally inherits a development shortcut.

# compose.override.yaml — applied automatically on top of compose.yaml
services:
  web:
    volumes:
      - .:/app          # live code reload in dev
    environment:
      DEBUG: "true"

# explicit, for a production-style run that ignores the override:
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d
yaml
Later -f files merge over earlier ones; override is auto-loaded by default.
Tearing it all down cleanly

Because Compose tracks everything it created under a project name, cleanup is precise. `docker compose down` removes the containers and the default network but, just like the plain volume commands, leaves named volumes alone so your data survives a restart. When you genuinely want a clean slate — a fresh database, no leftover state — add `-v` to remove the named volumes too.

Make the distinction a habit. `down` is your everyday stop button and is safe to run constantly. `down -v` is destructive and is the command you reach for only when you intend to wipe the data, such as resetting a local environment to reproduce a bug from scratch.

docker compose down            # stop + remove containers and network (keeps volumes)
docker compose down -v         # ALSO delete named volumes — wipes your data
docker compose down --rmi local  # also remove images this project built
bash
Use plain down daily; reserve -v for a deliberate data wipe.
Where to go next

You can now express an entire multi-service application — services, build steps, volumes, networks, dependencies, health checks, and environment configuration — in one file, and operate it with a handful of `docker compose` commands. That is the standard way teams run multi-container apps on a single host and is the natural bridge toward orchestration tools like Kubernetes.

The best way to internalise it is to build a real stack. Open the free Docker playground, write the web-plus-database Compose file from this guide, add the health check, then run `up`, `logs`, and `down`. Once you can spin a multi-service app up and down with confidence, you have the core of modern container workflows in hand.

title: Kubernetes Pods and Deployments Explained
summary: Understand Pods, why you almost never run them directly, and how Deployments keep your app alive and updatable.
seo_title: Kubernetes Pods and Deployments — A Beginner's Hands-On Guide
seo_description: Learn what a Pod really is, why Deployments manage Pods for you, and how to scale and roll out updates with kubectl. Practise in a free Kubernetes playground.
seo_keywords: kubernetes, pods, deployments, replicaset, kubectl, scaling, rolling update, beginner
sections: A Pod is the unit Kubernetes runs

When people first meet Kubernetes they expect to launch containers, but the smallest thing Kubernetes actually schedules is a Pod. Think of a Pod as a thin wrapper around one container (occasionally two or three that genuinely belong together). Everything inside a Pod shares the same network identity and can reach each other over localhost, and they live and die as a single unit.

That sharing is the whole reason Pods exist. If your main container needs a tiny helper alongside it — say a process that ships logs somewhere — putting both in one Pod guarantees they sit on the same node and start and stop together. Most of the time, though, a Pod holds exactly one container, and you can read 'Pod' as 'my running app instance' without losing much.

kubectl run demo --image=nginx:1.27 --restart=Never
kubectl get pods
kubectl get pod demo -o wide
bash
kubectl run with --restart=Never creates a bare Pod — useful for learning, rare in production.
Why a bare Pod is fragile

Create a Pod the way we just did and it will run — until it doesn't. Delete it, or let the node it sits on reboot, and nothing brings it back. A Pod has no memory of wanting to exist; it is a single, mortal instance. Run a quick experiment: delete the Pod and watch that nothing replaces it.

This is the gap that trips up newcomers. You did not do anything wrong, but a self-healing system should notice the app is gone and restore it. A bare Pod gives you none of that. What you actually want is something that holds the intent 'I always want N copies of this running' and acts on your behalf — and that something is a Deployment.

kubectl delete pod demo
kubectl get pods
# (empty — nothing recreated it)
bash
A standalone Pod, once deleted, stays gone. That is the problem Deployments solve.
Deployments declare desired state

A Deployment is the object you create in real life. Instead of saying 'start this Pod now', you write down the state you want — how many replicas, which image, which labels — and Kubernetes works continuously to make reality match. If a Pod crashes or its node disappears, the Deployment notices the replica count is short and creates a replacement, no human required.

The manifest below is the everyday shape you will write a hundred times. The `selector` tells the Deployment which Pods it owns (by matching labels), and the `template` is the Pod blueprint it stamps out. Keep the labels in `selector.matchLabels` and `template.metadata.labels` identical — a mismatch there is one of the most common beginner errors.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: hello
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
yaml
Save as hello-deploy.yaml, then run: kubectl apply -f hello-deploy.yaml
The ReplicaSet in the middle

When you apply that Deployment, three Pods appear. But there is a quiet third object between them: the ReplicaSet. A Deployment does not babysit Pods directly — it creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet's only job is to keep exactly the requested number of identical Pods running. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets; each ReplicaSet manages Pods.

You rarely touch ReplicaSets by hand, but it helps to know they are there, because they explain how rollouts work later. List all three layers and you will see the ownership chain: one Deployment, one ReplicaSet, three Pods whose names start with the ReplicaSet's name.

kubectl get deployments
kubectl get replicasets
kubectl get pods --show-labels
bash
Notice the Pod names: hello-<replicaset-hash>-<random>. That hash links them to their ReplicaSet.
Scaling up and down

Because the Deployment owns the replica count, changing how many copies run is a one-line change. You can edit the manifest and re-apply it (the declarative way, best for real projects since the file stays the source of truth), or scale imperatively for a quick adjustment. Both reach the same end state.

After scaling, watch the Pods settle. Kubernetes will add or remove Pods until the live count equals what you asked for, then stop. There is nothing to babysit — you state the number and the system converges on it.

# imperative: quick and handy while learning
kubectl scale deployment hello --replicas=5

# declarative: change replicas in the YAML, then
kubectl apply -f hello-deploy.yaml

kubectl get pods -l app=hello
bash
The -l flag filters to Pods carrying the app=hello label.
Rolling out a new version

Updating the image is where Deployments earn their keep. Change the image and Kubernetes performs a rolling update: it spins up new Pods with the new image and removes old ones gradually, so the app never goes fully dark. If the new version is broken, you can roll straight back to the previous ReplicaSet.

This is the payoff of the ReplicaSet layer from earlier — each version gets its own ReplicaSet, so 'undo' is just pointing back at the old one. Watch the rollout status to see Pods cut over, and try a rollback to feel how safe it is.

kubectl set image deployment/hello hello=nginx:1.28
kubectl rollout status deployment/hello

# changed your mind? go back one revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/hello
bash
rollout status blocks until the new Pods are healthy or the rollout stalls.
Reading a Pod's status when things go wrong

Sooner or later a Pod will not become Ready, and your first two commands are always the same: `describe` the Pod to read its recent events, and pull its logs. The Events section at the bottom of `describe` is the single most useful debugging output in Kubernetes — it tells you whether an image failed to pull, a probe failed, or the scheduler could not place the Pod.

Get into this habit now, while the stakes are low. Ninety percent of everyday troubleshooting is just reading these two outputs carefully before changing anything.

kubectl describe pod -l app=hello
kubectl logs -l app=hello --tail=50
# for a specific Pod by name:
kubectl logs hello-abc123-def45
bash
Scroll to the Events section of describe output first — it usually names the problem.
Try it in the playground

The ideas here only stick once you watch the system react.
