Open the Kubernetes playground and run the full arc: apply the Deployment, delete a Pod and watch it come back, scale the replicas up and down, then roll the image forward and undo it. Seeing Kubernetes restore desired state on its own is the moment the declarative model clicks.

title: Kubernetes Services and Ingress: Routing Traffic to Your Pods
summary: Give your Pods a stable address with Services, then expose HTTP routes to the outside world with Ingress.
seo_title: Kubernetes Services and Ingress — Networking Explained with Examples
seo_description: Learn how ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Services give Pods a stable address, and how an Ingress routes HTTP traffic by host and path. With runnable kubectl and YAML examples.
seo_keywords: kubernetes, service, clusterip, nodeport, loadbalancer, ingress, networking, kubectl, dns
sections: The problem Services solve

Pods are deliberately disposable. They get created and destroyed during scaling, updates, and node failures, and each one comes up with a fresh IP address. If you hard-coded a Pod's IP into another component, it would break the next time that Pod was replaced — which could be minutes later. You need a stable address that survives the churn beneath it.

A Service is that stable address. It gives a fixed name and IP to a logical group of Pods and load-balances requests across whichever of them are currently alive. Callers talk to the Service; the Service deals with the constantly shifting set of Pods behind it. This decoupling is what makes a Kubernetes app resilient instead of brittle.

kubectl get pods -l app=hello -o wide
# note the Pod IPs, then delete one and watch the new Pod get a different IP
kubectl delete pod -l app=hello --field-selector=status.phase=Running --grace-period=0 2>/dev/null
kubectl get pods -l app=hello -o wide
bash
Pod IPs change on recreation — never depend on them directly.
How a Service finds its Pods

A Service does not list Pods by name. Instead it uses a label selector: 'send traffic to every Pod carrying these labels'. As Pods come and go, Kubernetes keeps the Service's set of backend endpoints in sync automatically. This is the same label-matching idea that Deployments use, applied to networking.

The manifest below creates a ClusterIP Service (the default type) that targets every Pod labelled `app: hello`. Note the two ports: `port` is the address the Service answers on, and `targetPort` is the port inside the Pod it forwards to. They are often the same, but separating them lets you change one side without the other.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  selector:
    app: hello
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP
yaml
Apply it, then inspect the live endpoints with: kubectl get endpoints hello
ClusterIP: the default, internal address

A ClusterIP Service is reachable only from inside the cluster. That sounds limiting, but it is exactly what you want for the majority of services — a backend API, a database, a cache — that should never be exposed to the public internet and only ever talk to other Pods.

The real magic is DNS. Kubernetes gives every Service a DNS name, so from any Pod you can reach the `hello` Service simply by its name. You never look up an IP. This is why microservices can refer to each other by short, human-readable names that keep working as everything underneath scales and reschedules.

# from inside any Pod in the same namespace:
curl http://hello

# fully qualified form across namespaces:
curl http://hello.default.svc.cluster.local
bash
Service DNS name = <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local; within a namespace just <service> works.
NodePort and LoadBalancer: reaching in from outside

When traffic must come from outside the cluster, you change the Service type. A NodePort opens a high-numbered port (30000–32767) on every node, so anything that can reach a node's IP on that port lands on your Service. It is simple and great for learning or on-prem clusters, but exposing raw node ports is clumsy for real traffic.

A LoadBalancer goes further: on a cloud provider it provisions an external load balancer with its own public IP and points it at the Service. This is the clean way to expose a single service publicly. The catch is that one LoadBalancer per service gets expensive and gives you no smart routing — which is the gap Ingress fills.

# expose the existing Service externally via a node port
kubectl patch service hello -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
kubectl get service hello
# look for the PORT(S) column, e.g. 80:31423/TCP
bash
On a cloud cluster you would use type LoadBalancer; NodePort is the portable demo option.
Ingress: smart HTTP routing at the edge

Once you have more than one or two services to expose, paying for a load balancer per service and losing path-based routing stops making sense. An Ingress is a single entry point that routes incoming HTTP and HTTPS traffic to different Services based on the request's host and URL path. One public address, many backends.

Crucially, an Ingress is only a set of routing rules — it does nothing on its own. You also need an Ingress controller (such as the NGINX ingress controller) running in the cluster to read those rules and actually proxy traffic. People often forget the controller and wonder why their Ingress object exists but nothing responds.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80
yaml
Requests to /api go to the api Service; everything else to web — all through one address.
How the pieces fit together

It helps to picture the chain from the outside in. A user's request hits the Ingress controller at the cluster edge. The controller matches the host and path against your Ingress rules and forwards the request to the right Service. The Service load-balances it across the healthy Pods carrying the matching labels. The Pod handles the request.

Each layer has one job: the Ingress decides which service, the Service decides which Pod, and the Pod does the work. When something is unreachable, walk this chain in order — controller, Ingress rules, Service endpoints, Pod readiness — and you will find the break far faster than guessing.

# trace the chain when traffic does not arrive
kubectl get ingress
kubectl describe ingress shop
kubectl get endpoints web        # are there any Pod IPs behind the Service?
kubectl get pods -l app=web
bash
Empty endpoints almost always mean the Service selector does not match any Ready Pod's labels.
A common gotcha: selector mismatch

By far the most frequent networking bug is a Service whose selector does not match the Pods' labels. The Service exists, has a tidy ClusterIP, and DNS resolves — but it has zero endpoints, so every request times out. There is no error to see in the Service itself; you have to check its endpoints.

Whenever a Service is unreachable, the first command is `kubectl get endpoints <service>`. If the endpoint list is empty, the problem is almost certainly that the labels in `spec.selector` do not exactly match the labels on the Pods you expect to serve. Fix the labels on either side until they agree, and the endpoints populate immediately.

kubectl get endpoints hello
# compare the Service selector with the Pods' actual labels
kubectl get service hello -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pods --show-labels
bash
Selector and Pod labels must match exactly, including every key/value pair.
Practise the routing layer

Open the Kubernetes playground and build the path from Pod to public route yourself: create a Service in front of a Deployment, confirm it has endpoints, reach it by DNS from another Pod, then add an Ingress and route two paths to two different Services. Break the selector on purpose and watch the endpoints vanish — that one experiment will save you hours later.

title: Configuration and Health in Kubernetes: ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Probes
summary: Keep configuration out of your image, handle sensitive values safely, and teach Kubernetes when your app is actually ready.
seo_title: Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Probes — Configuration and Health Checks
seo_description: Externalise configuration with ConfigMaps, manage credentials with Secrets, and use liveness, readiness, and startup probes so Kubernetes knows your app's true state.
seo_keywords: kubernetes, configmap, secret, liveness probe, readiness probe, startup probe, environment variables, health check
sections: Why configuration does not belong in the image

A container image should be built once and run unchanged everywhere — dev, staging, production. The moment you bake an environment-specific value like a database URL or a feature flag into the image, you break that promise: now you need a different image per environment, and a config change forces a rebuild. That is slow and error-prone.

Kubernetes separates the application (the image) from its configuration (data that lives in the cluster). You inject configuration into the Pod at runtime, so the same image picks up different settings in different places. The two objects for this are ConfigMaps for ordinary configuration and Secrets for sensitive values.

# the same image, configured differently per environment
# image: myapp:1.0   (never changes between envs)
# config: provided by a ConfigMap/Secret at runtime
yaml
Build the image once; vary the configuration around it.
Storing plain configuration in a ConfigMap

A ConfigMap is a named bag of key/value pairs for non-sensitive settings: log levels, feature flags, hostnames, tunables. You define it once and reference it from any number of Pods. Because it is a first-class object, you can update configuration without touching your Deployment's image at all.

You can create a ConfigMap from literals on the command line for quick work, or declare it in YAML so it lives in version control alongside everything else. The declarative form is preferable for real projects because the file becomes the reviewable source of truth.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  FEATURE_DARK_MODE: "true"
  GREETING: "Hello from the cluster"
yaml
Quick alternative: kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info
Injecting a ConfigMap into a Pod

There are two common ways to get a ConfigMap into a container. The first is as environment variables, which suits flat key/value settings and is the most common choice. The second is as files mounted into a volume, which suits whole config files (an nginx.conf, an application.yaml) where your program expects to read from disk.

The snippet below uses `envFrom` to expose every key in the ConfigMap as an environment variable. After applying it, exec into the Pod and print the environment to confirm the values arrived. Remember that environment variables are read at container startup — changing the ConfigMap does not update a running Pod's env until it restarts.

spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
      # or mount as files:
      # volumeMounts:
      #   - name: cfg
      #     mountPath: /etc/app
  # volumes:
  #   - name: cfg
  #     configMap:
  #       name: app-config
yaml
Verify with: kubectl exec <pod> -- printenv | grep -E 'LOG_LEVEL|GREETING'
Secrets: same idea, for sensitive values

A Secret looks almost identical to a ConfigMap but is meant for passwords, API tokens, and TLS keys. Kubernetes treats Secrets with a little more care — they are not printed in casual output and can be encrypted at rest — and keeping them separate signals intent to your team and tooling.

One honest caveat that surprises newcomers: by default a Secret's values are only base64-encoded, not encrypted. Base64 is encoding, not security — anyone with read access can decode it instantly. Treat Secrets as 'values that need restricted access and encryption at rest', lock down who can read them with RBAC, and never commit raw Secret manifests to git.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
type: Opaque
stringData:
  DB_USER: appuser
  DB_PASSWORD: s3cr3t-rotate-me
yaml
stringData takes plain text and encodes it for you; never store the real password in git.
Consuming a Secret safely

You inject Secrets into Pods the same way as ConfigMaps — as environment variables or mounted files. For credentials, mounting as files is often safer than environment variables, because env vars can leak into logs, crash dumps, and child processes more easily. Either way, your application reads the value at runtime and the image stays clean.

The example pulls individual keys from the Secret into named environment variables using `valueFrom`, which is handy when you only want one or two values rather than the whole Secret. Pair this with RBAC so only the workloads and people who genuinely need the Secret can read it.

spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:1.0
      env:
        - name: DB_USER
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-credentials
              key: DB_USER
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-credentials
              key: DB_PASSWORD
yaml
valueFrom + secretKeyRef pulls a single key; useful when you do not want every key exposed.
Probes: teaching Kubernetes what 'healthy' means

A running container is not the same as a working application. A process can be up while the app inside is deadlocked, still warming up, or unable to serve requests. Kubernetes cannot read your app's mind, so you tell it how to check, using probes. There are three, each answering a different question.

A readiness probe answers 'can this Pod receive traffic right now?' — if it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints until it passes again, but the Pod is not restarted. A liveness probe answers 'is this container wedged and in need of a restart?' — if it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes kills and restarts the container. A startup probe answers 'has a slow-starting app finished booting yet?' — it holds off the other probes until the app is up, so a long boot is not mistaken for a failure.

# the three questions, in plain terms
# readiness  -> should traffic be sent here yet?   (fail = remove from Service)
# liveness   -> is it stuck and needing a restart? (fail = restart container)
# startup    -> has a slow boot finished?          (fail = keep waiting, no restart)
yaml
Readiness gates traffic; liveness triggers restarts; startup protects slow boots.
Wiring probes into a container

Probes are declared per container. The most common style is an HTTP GET against a health endpoint your app exposes, but you can also run a command (`exec`) or check a TCP port. Tune the timing fields so you do not restart a healthy-but-busy app: `initialDelaySeconds` waits before the first check, `periodSeconds` sets the interval, and `failureThreshold` sets how many misses count as a failure.

A classic mistake is pointing a liveness probe at an endpoint that depends on a downstream service. If the database hiccups, your liveness probe fails, Kubernetes restarts the Pod, and the restart does nothing to fix the database — you have turned a transient blip into a restart loop. Keep liveness checks shallow (is this process responsive?) and put dependency checks in readiness.

spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /ready
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 10
        failureThreshold: 3
      startupProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        failureThreshold: 30
        periodSeconds: 5
yaml
Keep liveness shallow; let readiness gate on dependencies so a blip doesn't cause restart loops.
Put it together in the playground

Open the Kubernetes playground and connect all three ideas: create a ConfigMap and a Secret, inject them into a Deployment, and confirm the values land inside the Pod with printenv. Then add readiness and liveness probes and watch how a failing readiness probe quietly pulls the Pod out of its Service while a failing liveness probe restarts it. Feeling that difference once is worth more than reading it ten times.

title: Troubleshooting Kubernetes: CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, and Friends
summary: A systematic playbook for diagnosing the Pod states that stall every Kubernetes user — read the signals before you change anything.
seo_title: Troubleshooting Kubernetes Pods — CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, and ImagePullBackOff
seo_description: A practical, systematic guide to diagnosing stuck Kubernetes Pods: CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, ImagePullBackOff, and OOMKilled — with the exact kubectl commands to find the cause.
seo_keywords: kubernetes, crashloopbackoff, pending pod, imagepullbackoff, oomkilled, troubleshooting, kubectl describe, debugging, events
sections: Debugging is reading, not guessing

When a Pod misbehaves, the instinct is to start changing things — bump the image, restart the Deployment, add resources. Resist it. Kubernetes is a declarative system that already records why it is doing what it is doing; your job is to read those records before you touch anything. Almost every Pod problem announces its own cause if you look in the right place.

This tutorial is a playbook. The Pod's STATUS column names the symptom; three commands almost always reveal the cause. Learn to map a status to its likely culprits and you will fix issues in minutes that otherwise eat an afternoon.

kubectl get pods
# the STATUS column is your starting point:
# CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, ...
bash
Always start from the STATUS column — it names the category of problem.
The three commands you will run every time

Whatever the symptom, your investigation begins with the same trio. `kubectl describe pod` shows the Pod's full state and, at the bottom, an Events list — the scheduler's and kubelet's own notes about what they tried and what failed. `kubectl logs` shows what the application itself printed, including the previous container with `--previous` (essential for a crashed Pod, since the current one may be too young to log anything). And `kubectl get events` shows cluster-wide activity sorted by time.

Commit these to muscle memory. The Events section of `describe` is the single highest-value output in Kubernetes troubleshooting — it will say 'Failed to pull image', 'Insufficient cpu', 'Liveness probe failed', or 'OOMKilled' in plain language, pointing you straight at the next step.

kubectl describe pod <pod>
kubectl logs <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous     # logs from the last crashed container
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
bash
logs --previous is how you read a container that has already crashed and restarted.
CrashLoopBackOff: the app starts, then dies

CrashLoopBackOff does not mean Kubernetes is broken — it means your container keeps starting and then exiting, and Kubernetes is restarting it with an increasing back-off delay (10s, 20s, 40s...) to avoid hammering. The container ran; the application inside failed. The fix is in your app, not the cluster.

Go straight to the previous container's logs — they hold the crash. Common causes are a missing or wrong environment variable or Secret, a config file the app cannot find, a failed connection to a dependency at startup, or simply a bad command/entrypoint that exits immediately. A subtler cause is a too-aggressive liveness probe killing a healthy-but-slow app; if `describe` shows 'Liveness probe failed' events, fix the probe timing rather than the app.

kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}{"\n"}'
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 -i 'liveness\|state\|exit'
bash
Read the previous logs first; check for an aggressive liveness probe as a secondary cause.
Pending: the Pod cannot be placed

A Pending Pod has been accepted by Kubernetes but not yet scheduled onto any node — it isn't even trying to start its container. The cause is always a placement problem, and the Events on `describe` will state it outright, usually beginning with 'FailedScheduling'.

The usual suspects: no node has enough free CPU or memory to satisfy the Pod's requests ('Insufficient cpu/memory'); the Pod requests a PersistentVolumeClaim that has not been bound; a nodeSelector, affinity rule, or taint means no node qualifies; or the cluster is simply at capacity and needs more nodes. The fix depends on which message you see — lower the resource requests, fix the PVC, relax the scheduling constraints, or add capacity — but you do not guess, you read the FailedScheduling reason.

kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A10 Events
# look for: 0/3 nodes are available: Insufficient cpu, ...
kubectl get pvc                       # is a claim still Pending?
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 'Allocated resources'
bash
Pending = scheduling failure. The FailedScheduling event names exactly what blocked placement.
ImagePullBackOff: Kubernetes can't get the image

ImagePullBackOff (and its sibling ErrImagePull) means the node tried to download the container image and failed, so it is backing off before retrying. This happens before the application ever runs, so application logs will be empty — the answer is in the Events, not the logs.

Walk the short checklist: is the image name and tag spelled correctly (a typo or a tag that does not exist is the most common cause)? Is the registry private and missing an imagePullSecret, giving an authorization error? Or can the node not reach the registry at all due to a network or DNS issue? The exact wording in the Events distinguishes 'not found', 'unauthorized', and 'no such host' for you.

kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 -i 'image\|pull'
# typical event lines:
#   Failed to pull image "myrepo/app:v9": not found
#   pull access denied ... unauthorized
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'
bash
Empty app logs + ImagePullBackOff means check the image name, tag, and registry credentials.
OOMKilled and resource limits

If a container shows a Terminated reason of OOMKilled, the Linux kernel killed it for exceeding its memory limit. This is not a leak in Kubernetes — it is your container using more memory than its `resources.limits.memory` allows, or a genuine memory leak in the app. A Pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff whose previous state is OOMKilled is a leak or an under-provisioned limit, restarting forever.

Decide which it is before reacting. If the app legitimately needs more memory, raise the limit (and the request, so the scheduler reserves it). If memory grows without bound under steady load, you have a leak to fix in the application. Setting requests too low also causes Pending elsewhere, so treat requests and limits as a deliberate pair, not an afterthought.
yaml
OOMKilled = over the memory limit. Distinguish 'limit too low' from 'app leaks memory'.
Running, but not Ready

Sometimes a Pod shows Running with 0/1 in the READY column. The container is up but its readiness probe is failing, so Kubernetes is correctly keeping it out of Service endpoints — which is why traffic 'mysteriously' never arrives. This is the system protecting you from sending requests to an app that says it is not ready.

Check the readiness probe events on `describe`, then confirm the health endpoint actually returns success from inside the Pod. Often the probe path, port, or expected status is wrong, or the app's readiness genuinely depends on a downstream that is itself down. Fix the probe or the dependency; do not 'fix' it by deleting the probe, which just hides the real problem.

kubectl get pod <pod>            # READY shows 0/1 while STATUS is Running
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A3 -i readiness
kubectl exec <pod> -- wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/ready || echo 'readiness endpoint failing'
bash
Running + 0/1 Ready means a failing readiness probe is correctly gating traffic.
When the Pod looks fine but traffic doesn't flow

If every Pod is Running and Ready yet requests still fail, the problem has moved up a layer to Services and networking. The fastest check is the Service's endpoints: an empty endpoints list means the Service's label selector matches no Ready Pod, so it has nothing to route to. This is the most common 'my app is up but unreachable' cause.

From there, walk outward: confirm the Service ports map to the right container port, that DNS resolves the Service name from another Pod, and — if you use one — that the Ingress rules and controller are healthy. Methodically following Pod, then Service endpoints, then Ingress isolates the break instead of leaving you poking at random.

kubectl get endpoints <service>       # empty = selector matches no Ready Pod
kubectl get service <service> -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{"\n"}'
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://<service>
bash
Empty endpoints is the number-one 'Pod is healthy but unreachable' culprit.
Build the reflex in the playground

Troubleshooting is a skill you build by doing, not reading. Open the Kubernetes playground and deliberately break things: deploy a Pod with a misspelled image, request more memory than any node has, point a readiness probe at a wrong port, and give a Service a selector that matches nothing. For each one, run describe, logs, and get events, and practise naming the cause from the output before you fix it. After a handful of reps, the STATUS column will tell you the story at a glance.

title: The Everyday Git Workflow: Add, Commit, Branch, Merge
summary: Build the daily loop every developer repeats: stage changes, commit them, branch off, and merge back.
seo_title: The Everyday Git Workflow — Add, Commit, Branch, and Merge Explained
seo_description: Learn the daily Git loop step by step: how staging works, how to write good commits, and how to branch and merge without fear. A hands-on beginner guide.
seo_keywords: git workflow, git add, git commit, git branch, git merge, staging area, fast-forward merge, beginner git
sections: A repository is a folder with a memory

Most tools forget the past the moment you hit save. Git does the opposite: it keeps a permanent, searchable record of every version of your project and who changed what. That record lives inside a hidden `.git` directory at the root of your project, and the folder that contains it is called a repository.

You turn any ordinary folder into a repository with a single command. Nothing leaves your machine and nothing is uploaded anywhere until you explicitly ask Git to talk to a remote server, so it is completely safe to experiment.

mkdir invoice-tool
cd invoice-tool
git init
# Initialized empty Git repository in .../invoice-tool/.git/
bash
git init only has to be run once per project.
Three places your work can live

The single biggest source of confusion for newcomers is that a changed file can be in one of three places, and Git treats each differently. The working directory is the set of files you actually edit. The staging area (also called the index) is a holding pen where you assemble the exact set of changes you want to save next. The repository is the permanent history of saved snapshots, called commits.

The reason for the middle step is control. You almost never want to save absolutely everything you touched in one lump. Staging lets you hand-pick which changes belong together so each commit tells one clear story.

git status
# Untracked files:
#   (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
#         invoice.py
#         scratch_notes.txt
bash
git status is the command you will run more than any other — it shows what is where.
Staging exactly what you mean to save

`git add` copies the current state of a file into the staging area. You can add one file, several files, or a whole directory. The dot shorthand `git add .` stages everything that changed beneath your current folder, which is convenient but blunt — it is easy to sweep in a stray debug file or some scratch notes you never meant to commit.

A habit worth forming early: stage deliberately and then run `git status` again to confirm the staging area holds what you expect. If you stage something by accident, `git restore --staged <file>` puts it back without touching your edits.

git add invoice.py          # stage one specific file
git status                  # confirm only invoice.py is staged
git restore --staged invoice.py   # changed your mind? unstage it
bash
Stage on purpose; reserve git add . for when you really do want everything.
Committing: turning staged changes into history

A commit is a permanent snapshot of whatever was in the staging area, stamped with your name, the time, and a message describing the change. Once committed, that version is safe — you can always come back to it. The message is not paperwork; it is the note your future self reads at 2am trying to understand why something changed.

Write messages in the imperative mood, as if completing the sentence 'This commit will…': 'Add tax calculation', 'Fix off-by-one in line totals'. Keep the first line under about fifty characters as a summary, and if more explanation is needed, leave a blank line and write a paragraph beneath it.

git commit -m "Add tax calculation to invoice totals"

# Need to explain the why as well as the what?
git commit   # opens your editor for a full summary + body
bash
Good commit messages are the cheapest documentation you will ever write.
Branches: parallel timelines that cost nothing

A branch is just a movable label pointing at a commit. Because creating one is instant and free, branches are the normal way to work on anything: a feature, a bug fix, an experiment. You branch off the main line, do your work in isolation, and the main branch stays clean and releasable the whole time.

The command `git switch -c <name>` creates a branch and moves you onto it in one step. (Older guides use `git checkout -b`; `switch` is the newer, clearer verb for changing branches.) While you are on the branch, every commit you make is recorded on it alone.

git switch -c add-discounts   # create the branch and move onto it
# ...edit files, stage, commit a few times...
git branch                    # list branches; * marks where you are
#   main
# * add-discounts
bash
Keep branches short-lived and focused on one piece of work.
Merging your branch back into main

When the work on a branch is finished, you bring its commits back into `main` with a merge. The rule that trips people up: you merge *into* the branch you are currently on, so switch to `main` first, then merge the feature branch into it.

If nothing else changed on `main` while you were away, Git performs a fast-forward — it simply slides the `main` label up to your latest commit, because there is nothing to reconcile. If `main` did move on, Git creates a new merge commit that ties the two lines of history together. Either way, once merged you can safely delete the feature branch; its commits now live on `main`.

git switch main
git merge add-discounts
# Fast-forward (or a merge commit if main advanced)

git branch -d add-discounts   # tidy up the merged branch
bash
Switch to the destination branch first, then merge the feature branch into it.
A complete cycle from start to finish

Here is the whole loop in one place — the rhythm you will repeat thousands of times. Initialize once, then for each piece of work: branch, edit, stage, commit (perhaps several times), switch back, and merge. Reading it end to end makes the shape of the workflow obvious.

The fastest way to internalize this is to type it out on a throwaway project. Make a folder, run these commands, and watch `git status` and `git log --oneline` after each step so you can see the state change. The model clicks the moment you have driven it yourself once.

git init                       # 1. start the repository (once)
git switch -c feature-x        # 2. branch off main
echo 'print("hi")' > app.py    #    do some work
git add app.py                 # 3. stage the change
git commit -m "Add app entrypoint"  # 4. commit it
git switch main                # 5. return to main
git merge feature-x            # 6. merge the work in
git log --oneline              #    read the resulting history
bash
The everyday loop: branch, edit, add, commit, switch, merge.

title: Git Rebase and Resolving Merge Conflicts
summary: Replay your commits onto fresh history, keep a clean log, and work calmly through conflicts when two changes collide.
seo_title: Git Rebase and Resolving Merge Conflicts — A Practical Intermediate Guide
seo_description: Understand the difference between merge and rebase, learn to rebase a feature branch safely, and resolve merge conflicts step by step with confidence.
seo_keywords: git rebase, merge conflicts, resolve conflicts, rebase vs merge, interactive rebase, git pull rebase, conflict markers
sections: Merge versus rebase: two ways to combine work

Both merge and rebase answer the same question — 'how do I bring the changes from one branch into another?' — but they produce very different histories. A merge preserves exactly what happened: it ties two lines of development together with a merge commit, so the log shows the branches diverging and reconverging.

A rebase instead rewrites your branch as if you had started it from a newer point. It lifts your commits off their original base and replays them, one by one, on top of the target branch. The result is a single straight line of history with no merge commit. Neither is universally correct: merges are honest about how work actually unfolded, while rebases give you a tidy, linear story that is easier to read later.

# Merge keeps the branch shape:
git switch main
git merge feature

# Rebase produces a straight line instead:
git switch feature
git rebase main
bash
Same goal, different history: one branching graph versus one straight line.
What rebase actually does, commit by commit

Imagine you branched off `main` last week and made three commits. Meanwhile your teammates added five commits to `main`. Your branch is now based on a stale starting point. A rebase takes your three commits, temporarily sets them aside, fast-forwards your branch to the latest `main`, and then re-applies your three commits on top — creating three brand-new commits with new identifiers but the same changes.

The key consequence is that rebasing rewrites history: the replayed commits are not the same objects as the originals. That is harmless and desirable for commits that live only on your own machine. It becomes a problem only when others have already based work on the commits you are about to rewrite, which is the subject of the golden rule a few sections down.

git switch feature
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# First, rewinding head to replay your work on top of it...
# Applying: Add discount field
# Applying: Validate discount range
# Applying: Show discount on receipt
bash
Your commits are replayed onto the latest base — new commits, same changes.
Why a conflict happens at all

A conflict is not an error or a sign you did something wrong. It simply means two changes both touched the same lines of the same file, and Git cannot know which one you intended to win — so it stops and asks you. This can happen during a merge or during a rebase; the resolution process is nearly identical.

Git marks the contested region inside the file with three sets of markers. Everything between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` is one side's version; everything between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` is the other side's. Your job is to edit that region into the single version you actually want and then delete all three marker lines.

<<<<<<< HEAD
tax_rate = 0.07
=======
tax_rate = 0.0725
>>>>>>> feature
# Decide the real value, delete all marker lines, keep one clean line.
text
The markers show both sides; you produce the final, correct version.
Resolving a conflict, step by step

When Git stops on a conflict, do not panic and do not abort by reflex. Run `git status` — it lists exactly which files are 'unmerged' and need your attention. Open each one, find the marker regions, and edit them down to the correct final content with no markers left behind.

Once a file looks right, stage it with `git add` to tell Git 'this one is resolved'. When every conflicted file is staged, you finish the operation. During a merge you run `git commit`; during a rebase you run `git rebase --continue`, which re-applies the remaining commits. If things get confusing at any point, `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` returns you to exactly where you started, as if nothing happened.

git status                 # see which files are unmerged
# edit each conflicted file, removing the <<<< ==== >>>> markers
git add invoice.py         # mark this file as resolved

# finish a merge:        git commit
# finish a rebase:       git rebase --continue
# bail out entirely:     git rebase --abort
bash
Edit, git add to mark resolved, then continue — or abort to reset cleanly.
Rebase to keep a feature branch current

The most common everyday use of rebase is keeping a long-running feature branch up to date with `main` without cluttering its history with repeated merge commits. Instead of merging `main` into your branch every day, you rebase your branch onto the latest `main`. Your feature commits stay together at the tip, sitting cleanly on top of current work.

Many teams also configure pulls to rebase rather than merge, so that integrating remote changes never sprinkles tiny merge commits through the log. You can do this per-pull with a flag or set it as the default once.

git pull --rebase origin main   # integrate remote changes, stay linear

# Make it the default for every pull in this repo:
git config pull.rebase true
bash
Rebasing on pull keeps your local history a clean straight line.
Interactive rebase: cleaning up before you share

Interactive rebase lets you edit your own recent history before anyone else sees it: reorder commits, reword messages, drop a commit, or squash several scrappy 'wip' commits into one polished commit. You start it by telling Git how far back to go — for example, the last three commits.

Git opens an editor listing those commits with a verb beside each. Change `pick` to `squash` (or `s`) to fold a commit into the one above it, `reword` to fix a message, or `drop` to delete it entirely. Save and close, and Git replays the commits according to your instructions. This is how a messy local branch becomes a clean, reviewable series of commits.

git rebase -i HEAD~3

# editor opens:
# pick a1b2c3d Add discount field
# squash d4e5f6a fix typo
# squash 7a8b9c0 actually fix it this time
# -> becomes ONE tidy commit
bash
Squash 'wip' commits into one clean commit before opening a pull request.
The golden rule of rebasing shared history

Here is the one rule that keeps rebase from causing pain: never rebase commits that other people have already pulled. Because rebase rewrites commits into new objects, anyone who based work on the originals will find their history and yours have silently diverged, leading to duplicated commits and confusing forced-update conflicts.

The safe boundary is simple. Rebase freely while your commits are local or live only on a personal branch nobody else uses. Once you have pushed a branch that teammates pull from, prefer merging to integrate further changes. If you truly must rewrite an already-pushed branch, push it with `--force-with-lease`, which refuses to clobber work you have not seen — a far safer choice than a blunt `--force`.

# Safe: rewriting your own un-shared commits
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# Only if you MUST update an already-pushed branch you own:
git push --force-with-lease
# Avoid plain --force; it can silently overwrite others' work.
bash
Rebase private history freely; never rewrite commits others already rely on.

title: Undoing Mistakes in Git: Reset, Revert, and Reflog
summary: Recover from bad commits, accidental resets, and lost branches using the right tool for each situation.
seo_title: Undoing Mistakes in Git — Reset, Revert, and Reflog Done Right
seo_description: Master Git recovery: when to use reset vs revert, the difference between soft, mixed, and hard reset, and how the reflog rescues lost commits and branches.
seo_keywords: git reset, git revert, git reflog, undo commit, soft mixed hard reset, recover lost commits, git restore, detached head
sections: First, calm down: Git rarely loses anything

The reassuring truth behind almost every Git panic is that committed work is extraordinarily hard to actually lose. Once a change has been committed, Git keeps the underlying snapshot around for weeks even after you 'delete' it, and there is a hidden log that remembers everywhere your branch has ever pointed. Most 'I destroyed my work' moments are fully recoverable.

The danger zone is uncommitted work — edits sitting in your working directory that were never staged or committed. Those have no safety net. So the first move in any recovery situation is to commit or stash what you have, even into a throwaway commit, before you start undoing anything. With a snapshot in hand, you can experiment freely.

git stash            # park uncommitted edits safely out of the way
# ...do your recovery work...
git stash pop        # bring the edits back when ready
bash
Snapshot uncommitted work first — committed history is almost always recoverable.
Undo without rewriting history: git revert

When the bad commit has already been pushed and shared, you must undo its effect without erasing it from history, because rewriting shared history breaks everyone else's clones. `git revert` is built for exactly this. It does not delete the offending commit; instead it creates a brand-new commit that applies the inverse of those changes, cleanly cancelling them out while leaving the record intact.

This is the only safe way to undo something on a branch others rely on, such as `main`. The history grows forward — 'we did X, then we deliberately undid X' — which is honest and conflict-free for collaborators who simply pull the new commit.

git revert a1b2c3d        # create a commit that undoes a1b2c3d

# Undo a merge commit (pick the mainline parent with -m 1):
git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>
bash
revert is the safe, shareable undo: it adds an inverse commit rather than erasing.
Rewriting local history: the three faces of reset

`git reset` moves your current branch label to point at an older commit, effectively rewinding history. What makes it powerful — and occasionally dangerous — is the mode flag, which decides what happens to the changes from the commits you rewound past.

`--soft` moves the branch but leaves every change staged, as if you had just `git add`ed them. `--mixed` (the default) moves the branch and unstages the changes, leaving them as edits in your working directory. `--hard` moves the branch and throws the changes away entirely, matching your files to the target commit. Soft and mixed are non-destructive — your changes survive in the working tree — while hard discards working-directory changes, so reserve it for when you are certain.

git reset --soft  HEAD~1   # undo last commit; keep changes STAGED
git reset --mixed HEAD~1   # undo last commit; keep changes UNSTAGED
git reset --hard  HEAD~1   # undo last commit; DISCARD the changes
bash
soft keeps changes staged, mixed unstages them, hard deletes them.
The classic 'fix the last commit' moves

Two everyday mistakes have clean, idiomatic fixes. First: you committed too early and forgot a file, or your commit message has a typo. `git commit --amend` rewrites the most recent commit, folding in newly staged changes and letting you edit the message — as long as you have not pushed it yet.

Second: you committed to the wrong branch, or want to keep the work but drop the commit. A soft reset by one commit gives you back your changes, fully staged, so you can recommit them elsewhere or restage them differently. Pair these two and most 'oops' moments are a ten-second fix.

# Forgot a file in the last commit:
git add forgotten_file.py
git commit --amend --no-edit

# Keep the work but undo the commit itself:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
bash
Amend to patch the last commit; soft reset to un-commit while keeping the work.
Restoring files without touching history

Sometimes you do not want to move any branch at all — you just want a file back the way it was. The modern, purpose-built command for this is `git restore`. To throw away unstaged edits in a file and return it to its last committed state, restore it from HEAD. To pull a specific file out of an older commit without disturbing anything else, restore it from that commit.

Because `restore` only affects file contents and never moves branch pointers, it is far less error-prone than overloading `reset` or `checkout` for the same job. Use it whenever the question is 'I want this file to look like it did at commit X' rather than 'I want to rewind my whole branch.'

git restore app.py                 # discard unstaged edits in app.py
git restore --staged app.py        # unstage app.py, keep the edits
git restore --source=a1b2c3d app.py  # grab app.py from an old commit
bash
restore targets individual files; reset moves the whole branch pointer.
The reflog: Git's undo button for undo

The reflog is the safety net almost nobody knows about until it saves them. Every time your branch tip moves — a commit, a reset, a rebase, a checkout — Git quietly records the previous position in a local log. Even after a `git reset --hard` that seemingly vaporized commits, those commits still exist and the reflog remembers their identifiers.

Run `git reflog` to see a numbered list of every recent position of HEAD, each with a short description like 'reset: moving to HEAD~3'. Find the entry from just before your mistake, note its commit identifier, and you can jump back to it. This is how you recover from a hard reset that went too far or a rebase that mangled things.

git reflog
# a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# 9f8e7d6 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add discount validation   <- the good state
# 3c2b1a0 HEAD@{2}: commit: Add discount field
bash
The reflog lists every position HEAD has held — your map back to lost work.
Recovering lost commits and deleted branches

With a reflog entry in hand, recovery is straightforward. To restore your branch to a prior good state after a too-aggressive reset, hard-reset it back onto the identifier you found. To rescue commits that were orphaned — say you deleted a branch before merging — create a new branch pointing at the lost commit's identifier, and the commits spring back into a named branch.

This is why the earlier advice to commit early matters so much: the reflog only knows about states your branch actually pointed at. Work that was committed can almost always be brought back; work that was never committed cannot. Treat the reflog as your last line of defence, not your first — but know it is there.

# Undo a reset that went too far:
git reset --hard 9f8e7d6        # an id from git reflog

# Resurrect a branch you deleted before merging:
git branch recovered-feature 9f8e7d6
git switch recovered-feature
bash
Point a fresh branch at a reflog id to bring orphaned commits back to life.

title: Ansible Inventories and Ad-Hoc Commands
summary: Describe your fleet in an inventory and act on it instantly with one-line ad-hoc commands.
seo_title: Ansible Inventories and Ad-Hoc Commands — A Hands-On Beginner Guide
seo_description: Learn how to define hosts in an Ansible inventory, group them, and run instant ad-hoc commands with modules like ping, command, and package. Try it in a free playground.
seo_keywords: ansible, inventory, ad-hoc commands, hosts, groups, modules, ping, beginner, devops
sections: What an inventory actually is

Before Ansible can do anything useful it needs an answer to one question: which machines am I allowed to talk to? That answer lives in the inventory. An inventory is nothing more than a list of hosts, optionally bundled into named groups, written in a file you keep alongside your project.

Think of the inventory as the address book for your fleet. You write it once, commit it to version control, and from then on you refer to machines by friendly group names like webservers or dbservers instead of memorising IP addresses. Everything else in Ansible — ad-hoc commands, playbooks, roles — reads from this same list.

ansible --version
ansible-inventory --version
bash
Confirm Ansible is installed before going further.
Writing your first INI inventory

The quickest inventory format is INI-style: a group name in square brackets, followed by one host per line. A host can be a DNS name or an IP address. Lines that sit above any group header belong to an implicit ungrouped section, but it is cleaner to always name your groups.

Below, three machines are split into two groups. The same host can appear in more than one group, which is handy when a box plays multiple roles — for example a small server that is both a web node and a cache.

[web]
web1.lab.internal
web2.lab.internal

[db]
db1.lab.internal

[cache]
web2.lab.internal   # web2 also serves cache
ini
Save this as hosts.ini in your project directory.
Per-host and per-group variables

Hosts rarely behave identically. One might listen on a non-standard SSH port; another might need a specific Python interpreter. You attach these details as variables, either inline after the hostname or in a dedicated group block whose name ends in :vars.

Variables defined in a :vars block apply to every host in that group, while inline variables apply to a single host only. This keeps repetition out of your inventory: set the SSH user once for the whole group rather than on every line.

[web]
web1.lab.internal ansible_port=2222
web2.lab.internal

[web:vars]
ansible_user=deploy
ansible_python_interpreter=/usr/bin/python3
ini
Inline vars override group vars for that single host.
Verifying the inventory parses

A mistyped bracket or a stray space can silently drop a host from a group, so always confirm Ansible reads the file the way you intended. The ansible-inventory command renders the parsed result, and the --graph flag prints a readable tree of groups and their members.

Getting into the habit of running this check after every edit saves you from the classic confusion of a command that 'does nothing' simply because it matched zero hosts.

ansible-inventory -i hosts.ini --graph

# Or dump the full parsed data as JSON
ansible-inventory -i hosts.ini --list
bash
--graph shows the group tree; --list shows resolved variables.
Your first ad-hoc command

An ad-hoc command runs a single Ansible module against a set of hosts, right now, without writing a playbook. The shape is always the same: name a host pattern, choose a module with -m, and pass arguments with -a. It is the fastest way to answer 'is this host alive?' or 'what does uptime say across the whole fleet?'.

The ping module is the traditional first test. It is not an ICMP ping — it logs in over SSH and confirms Ansible can run Python on the target, which is exactly what every later task depends on.

# Ping every host in the inventory
ansible all -i hosts.ini -m ping

# Ping only the web group
ansible web -i hosts.ini -m ping
bash
'all' is a built-in pattern matching every host.
Running real work ad-hoc

Once connectivity is proven, ad-hoc commands become a powerful operations tool. The command module runs an arbitrary program on each host; the package module installs software. Tasks that change the system usually need elevated privileges, which you request with --become (Ansible's equivalent of sudo).

A useful detail: you can tune how many hosts run in parallel with -f (forks). On a large fleet, bumping the fork count makes a sweep across hundreds of machines finish in seconds rather than minutes.

# Check disk usage on every database host
ansible db -i hosts.ini -m command -a "df -h /"

# Install curl on the web group, with sudo, 20 at a time
ansible web -i hosts.ini -m package \
  -a "name=curl state=present" --become -f 20
bash
Use --become for anything that modifies the system.
Host patterns: targeting exactly what you mean

The first argument to ansible is a pattern, and it understands more than plain group names. You can combine groups with a colon for a union, exclude a group with an exclamation mark, and intersect two groups with an ampersand. This lets you express precise targets without editing the inventory.

For example, 'web:!cache' means every web host that is not also in the cache group. Mastering patterns means you spend less time maintaining one-off groups and more time describing intent directly on the command line.

# Union: every web OR db host
ansible 'web:db' -i hosts.ini -m ping

# Exclude: web hosts that are NOT in cache
ansible 'web:!cache' -i hosts.ini -m ping

# Intersection: hosts in BOTH web and cache
ansible 'web:&cache' -i hosts.ini -m ping
bash
Quote the pattern so the shell does not interpret the symbols.
Practise in the playground

You now have the two foundations everything else in Ansible builds on: an inventory that names your hosts, and ad-hoc commands that act on them instantly. The fastest way to make these stick is to type them yourself and watch the output.

Open the Ansible playground and run the version, ping, and help commands, then experiment with host patterns. When you are comfortable here, the next step is collecting commands into a repeatable playbook.

title: Writing Ansible Playbooks and Tasks
summary: Move from one-off commands to repeatable YAML playbooks built from ordered, idempotent tasks.
seo_title: Writing Ansible Playbooks and Tasks — Plays, Modules, Handlers
seo_description: Go beyond ad-hoc commands and write Ansible playbooks: plays, tasks, handlers, conditionals, loops, and idempotence. Includes runnable YAML examples and a free playground.
seo_keywords: ansible, playbook, tasks, plays, handlers, idempotence, when, loop, yaml, devops
sections: From ad-hoc to playbooks

Ad-hoc commands are perfect for a quick check, but they vanish the moment your terminal closes. A playbook captures the same work as a file you can read, review, version, and re-run forever. It is the difference between shouting an instruction across the room and writing down a recipe.

A playbook is a YAML document. At the top level it holds one or more plays, and each play maps a group of hosts to an ordered list of tasks. Because it is plain text, the playbook doubles as living documentation of exactly how a system should be configured.

ansible-playbook --version

# Always check syntax before a real run
ansible-playbook site.yml --syntax-check
bash
--syntax-check parses the file without touching any host.
Anatomy of a play

Every play answers three questions: which hosts, with what privileges, and which tasks. The hosts key takes any inventory pattern. The become key requests sudo for the whole play so you do not repeat it on every task. The tasks key holds the ordered list of work.

YAML is whitespace-sensitive, so indentation is not decoration — it defines structure. Use spaces, never tabs, and keep the indentation consistent. A list item begins with a dash, and a mapping is a set of key: value pairs. Get these two ideas right and the rest of the syntax follows naturally.

- name: Configure web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure nginx is installed
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: nginx
        state: present
yaml
The play's name and each task's name appear in the run output.
Tasks call modules to reach a desired state

A task is a single step that invokes one module. The crucial mental shift from shell scripting is that you describe the end state you want, not the commands to get there. Instead of 'run apt install nginx', you declare 'the nginx package should be present', and the module figures out whether any action is needed.

This is idempotence in practice. Run the playbook once and the package installs; run it again and the module reports 'ok' because the state already matches. You can re-run a playbook as many times as you like without fear of duplicating work or breaking something that is already correct.

tasks:
  - name: Ensure the app directory exists
    ansible.builtin.file:
      path: /opt/myapp
      state: directory
      owner: deploy
      mode: "0755"

  - name: Ensure nginx is running and enabled
    ansible.builtin.service:
      name: nginx
      state: started
      enabled: true
yaml
Each module reports changed only when it actually altered the host.
Handlers: act only when something changed

Some actions should run only as a consequence of a change. The classic case is restarting a service after its config file is edited — you do not want to restart nginx on every run, only when the config actually differs. Handlers solve this elegantly.

A handler is a task that lies dormant until another task notifies it. A task that reports changed fires its notify; handlers then run once, at the end of the play, no matter how many tasks notified them. This keeps restarts minimal and your runs fast.

tasks:
  - name: Deploy nginx config
    ansible.builtin.copy:
      src: nginx.conf
      dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    notify: Restart nginx

handlers:
  - name: Restart nginx
    ansible.builtin.service:
      name: nginx
      state: restarted
yaml
The handler runs once at the end, only if the copy changed.
Conditionals with when

Real fleets are heterogeneous: a task that makes sense on Debian may need a different package name on Red Hat. The when key attaches a condition to a task so it runs only when an expression is true. The expression is plain Jinja2 evaluated against gathered facts and variables.

Ansible automatically gathers facts about each host at the start of a play — its OS family, IP addresses, memory, and more — and exposes them under ansible_facts. Conditioning on these facts lets a single playbook adapt itself to every host it touches.

tasks:
  - name: Install Apache on Debian family
    ansible.builtin.package:
      name: apache2
      state: present
    when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == "Debian"

  - name: Install Apache on RedHat family
    ansible.builtin.package:
      name: httpd
      state: present
    when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == "RedHat"
yaml
Facts are collected automatically unless you disable gather_facts.
Loops: repeat a task over a list

When you need to apply the same module to many values — install five packages, create three users — a loop keeps the playbook short. The loop key takes a list, and each element is exposed inside the task as the special variable item.

Looping is more than a convenience: it keeps the desired state in one declarative list rather than copy-pasted blocks that drift apart over time. Add a package to the list and it is managed; remove it and the task stops touching it.

tasks:
  - name: Ensure base packages are installed
    ansible.builtin.package:
      name: "{{ item }}"
      state: present
    loop:
      - git
      - curl
      - htop
      - vim
yaml
{{ item }} holds the current element on each pass.
Running and reading the output

With the playbook written, run it with ansible-playbook and your inventory. Each task prints a colour-coded result: green ok means the host already matched, yellow changed means Ansible acted, and red means a failure that stops the play for that host. The PLAY RECAP at the end summarises counts per host.

Two flags are invaluable while developing. Use --check for a dry run that reports what would change without changing anything, and --diff to see the exact before-and-after of files and templates. Together they let you preview a deployment with confidence.

# Real run
ansible-playbook -i hosts.ini site.yml

# Dry run: predict changes without making them
ansible-playbook -i hosts.ini site.yml --check --diff
bash
Read the PLAY RECAP: ok vs changed vs failed per host.
Practise in the playground

You can now write a play, fill it with idempotent tasks, branch with when, repeat with loop, and restart services cleanly through handlers. That is the core of day-to-day Ansible. The next level is packaging this logic so it can be reused across projects.

Open the Ansible playground to run ansible-playbook and experiment with the commands above. When you are ready, the roles-and-templates tutorial shows how to turn a single playbook into a reusable, parameterised role.

title: Ansible Roles, Variables, and Templates
summary: Package automation into reusable roles, drive it with layered variables, and render config with Jinja2 templates.
seo_title: Ansible Roles, Variables, and Templates — Reusable Automation Done Right
seo_description: Structure Ansible into reusable roles, master variable precedence with defaults and vars, and generate dynamic config files with Jinja2 templates. Runnable examples included.
seo_keywords: ansible, roles, variables, templates, jinja2, defaults, vars, precedence, reusable, devops
sections: Why a single playbook stops scaling

A one-file playbook is fine for a weekend project, but as you manage more services it grows into a thousand-line wall of tasks that is hard to read, impossible to reuse, and risky to change. The answer is the same one software engineers reached long ago: break the monolith into modules. In Ansible, that module is the role.

A role is a standardised directory layout that bundles everything one piece of automation needs — its tasks, default variables, files, templates, and handlers — behind a single name. Once nginx lives in a role, any playbook on any project can pull it in with one line, and improvements to the role benefit everyone who uses it.

# Scaffold a new role with the standard layout
ansible-galaxy role init nginx
bash
ansible-galaxy creates the conventional directory structure for you.
The standard role directory layout

Ansible discovers a role's parts by convention, so the directory names matter. The most-used ones are tasks (the main list of work), defaults (the lowest-priority variables, meant to be overridden), vars (higher-priority variables), templates (Jinja2 files), files (static files to copy), and handlers.

When a role runs, Ansible automatically loads tasks/main.yml, defaults/main.yml, handlers/main.yml, and so on. You never spell out these paths in your tasks — referencing a template by filename is enough, because Ansible knows to look in the role's templates directory. This convention-over-configuration approach is what makes roles so portable.

roles/
  nginx/
    defaults/
      main.yml      # low-priority, overridable vars
    vars/
      main.yml      # high-priority vars
    tasks/
      main.yml      # the role's tasks
    templates/
      nginx.conf.j2 # Jinja2 templates
    handlers/
      main.yml      # notified handlers
text
Ansible auto-loads each main.yml inside the role.
Defaults vs vars: designing for overrides

Roles become reusable only when the people using them can adjust behaviour without editing the role itself. That is the purpose of defaults/main.yml: it holds sensible default values that callers are expected to override. Because role defaults sit at the very bottom of Ansible's precedence ladder, almost anything can replace them — inventory variables, playbook vars, or command-line extra-vars.

The vars/main.yml file is the opposite. It holds values the role considers fixed, and it sits near the top of precedence, so it is hard to override by accident. The practical rule is: put anything a user might reasonably want to tune in defaults, and reserve vars for internal constants the role depends on.

# roles/nginx/defaults/main.yml
nginx_worker_processes: auto
nginx_listen_port: 80
nginx_server_name: localhost

# roles/nginx/vars/main.yml
nginx_config_path: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf   # internal, fixed
yaml
Tune defaults from outside; treat vars as the role's internals.
Understanding variable precedence

Variables in Ansible can be set in many places, and when the same name is set twice the question is which value wins. Ansible resolves this with a fixed precedence order. Knowing the broad shape of it prevents hours of confused debugging.

From lowest to highest, the values you will touch most are: role defaults, then inventory group_vars, then inventory host_vars, then play vars, and finally extra-vars passed with -e on the command line, which beat everything. A reliable habit is to put baselines in role defaults and reach for -e only for genuine one-off overrides during a run.

# Role default says port 80...
# ...but this command-line override wins over everything
ansible-playbook site.yml -e "nginx_listen_port=8080"

# group_vars/web.yml would override the default but lose to -e
# group_vars/web.yml:
#   nginx_server_name: web.example.com
bash
-e (extra-vars) has the highest precedence of all.
Jinja2 templates: config that adapts itself

Hard-coding a port or a hostname into a config file defeats the point of variables. The template module renders a Jinja2 file on the controller, substituting your variables, and writes the result to each host. A template file conventionally ends in .j2 and lives in the role's templates directory.

Inside the template, {{ variable }} inserts a value, {% ... %} runs logic such as loops and conditionals, and {# ... #} is a comment. Because the same template is rendered fresh per host with that host's variables and facts, one template can produce a correct, customised config for every machine in your fleet.
jinja2
{{ }} substitutes values; {% %} runs logic like if-blocks.
Wiring the template into a task

A template is rendered by the template module, which takes src (the .j2 filename, found automatically in the role's templates folder) and dest (where to write the result on the target). Pair it with a notify so that whenever the rendered file actually changes, the relevant service restarts — exactly the handler pattern from playbooks, now inside a reusable role.

Because templates are rendered per host, you also get a free dry-run preview: run with --check --diff and Ansible shows the exact lines that would change in the generated config, with no risk to the live file.

# roles/nginx/tasks/main.yml
- name: Render nginx config from template
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: "{{ nginx_config_path }}"
    mode: "0644"
  notify: Restart nginx

# roles/nginx/handlers/main.yml
- name: Restart nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
yaml
src needs only the filename; Ansible finds it under templates/.
Using and parameterising the role

With the role complete, a playbook consumes it through the roles key, and it can pass values to override the defaults inline. The same role can appear in many playbooks with different settings — one play might run nginx on port 80, another on 8080, with no change to the role itself.

This is the payoff for all the structure: your top-level playbook becomes a short, readable list of which roles to apply to which hosts, while the messy detail stays neatly encapsulated. Roles are also the unit you share on Ansible Galaxy, so well-factored roles can be reused far beyond your own projects.

- name: Build the web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  roles:
    - role: nginx
      vars:
        nginx_listen_port: 8080
        nginx_server_name: app.example.com
        enable_gzip: true
yaml
Override defaults right where you include the role.
Practise in the playground

You can now structure automation the way professionals do: reusable roles with a conventional layout, a clear separation between overridable defaults and internal vars, an understanding of which variable wins, and Jinja2 templates that render correct config for every host. This is the foundation of maintainable, shareable infrastructure code.

Open the Ansible playground to run ansible-galaxy and ansible-playbook, and experiment with overriding variables via -e. From here you are well equipped to build and publish your own roles.

title: Bash Shell Scripting Fundamentals
summary: Write, run, and parameterize your first Bash scripts the right way, from the shebang to exit codes.
seo_title: Bash Shell Scripting Fundamentals — Write Your First Robust Scripts
seo_description: A beginner's guide to Bash scripting: the shebang, running scripts, comments, quoting, command output, and exit codes. Practise live in a free shell sandbox.
seo_keywords: bash, shell scripting, shebang, chmod, exit code, quoting, beginner, tutorial
sections: A script is just commands in a file

Anything you can type at a shell prompt, you can save in a file and run later. That is the whole premise of shell scripting: instead of retyping a sequence of commands every time, you record them once and replay them on demand. The payoff grows with every repetition — a five-line script you run daily saves you far more than the minute it took to write.

The first line of a real script is the shebang: a `#!` followed by the path to the interpreter that should run the file. Using `/usr/bin/env bash` rather than a hard-coded `/bin/bash` lets the system find Bash wherever it happens to be installed, which keeps the script portable across machines.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# hello.sh — my first script
echo "Hello from a Bash script"
echo "Today is $(date +%A)"
bash
The shebang must be the very first line, with no blank lines above it.
Making a script runnable

Creating the file is not enough — by default a fresh text file has no permission to execute. You grant that with `chmod +x`, which flips the executable bit so the kernel is allowed to run it. After that you invoke the script by giving its path, including the leading `./` when it lives in the current directory.

The `./` is not decoration. The shell only searches the directories listed in your `PATH` for bare command names, and the current directory is deliberately left out of `PATH` for safety. Spelling out `./hello.sh` tells the shell exactly which file you mean.

chmod +x hello.sh     # mark the file executable
./hello.sh            # run it from the current directory

# alternative: hand the file to bash directly (no +x needed)
bash hello.sh
bash
Running with `bash hello.sh` ignores the executable bit and the shebang.
Comments and readable layout

A comment starts with `#` and runs to the end of the line; Bash ignores everything after it. Comments are not just for explaining clever tricks — a one-line summary at the top of a script saying what it does and how to call it will save the next reader (often future you) real time.

Resist the urge to narrate the obvious. The best comments explain *why* a line exists, not *what* it does. A line like `rm -rf "$tmp"` does not need a comment saying 'remove the temp dir'; it might benefit from one saying 'safe because $tmp is always our own mktemp output'.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup.sh — copy the app config to a dated archive.
# Usage: ./backup.sh

src=/etc/myapp          # what we are backing up
dest=/var/backups       # where archives land

# Stamp the filename with the date so runs don't clobber each other.
tar -czf "$dest/myapp-$(date +%F).tar.gz" "$src"
bash
`date +%F` expands to an ISO date like 2026-06-23.
Capturing command output

Scripts become powerful when one command feeds another. Command substitution, written `$(...)`, runs a command and replaces the whole expression with whatever that command printed. You can store the result in a variable or drop it straight into another command.

The older backtick form `` `...` `` does the same thing, but `$(...)` is clearer and nests cleanly, so prefer it in new code. Whatever you capture, wrap the expansion in double quotes when you use it — that protects multi-word or empty results from being mangled by the shell.

now=$(date +%H:%M)
user_count=$(who | wc -l)
echo "At $now there are $user_count users logged in"

# Nesting reads naturally with $(...)
echo "Kernel: $(uname -r) on $(hostname)"
bash
`who | wc -l` counts logged-in sessions by counting lines.
Quoting: the habit that prevents most bugs

Quoting is where beginners get burned, so it pays to learn the rule early. Single quotes are literal — Bash changes nothing inside them. Double quotes allow variable and command expansion but still protect spaces. Unquoted text is split on whitespace and expanded as a filename pattern, which is almost never what you want for a variable.

The practical takeaway: put double quotes around your variable expansions unless you have a specific reason not to. `"$file"` survives spaces in filenames; bare `$file` will silently break the moment someone hands you `My Document.pdf`.
bash
The unquoted `touch` creating two files is the classic word-splitting trap.
Exit codes tell the rest of the world how it went

Every command finishes with an exit code: a number from 0 to 255 where 0 means success and anything else means some kind of failure. The shell stores the most recent code in the special variable `$?`. This convention is the glue that lets scripts, pipelines, and CI systems chain commands together and react to failures.

When you write a script, end it with a deliberate exit code so callers can trust it. `exit 0` says all is well; a non-zero `exit` signals trouble, ideally with a message sent to standard error so it shows up even when normal output is redirected away.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [[ ! -f /etc/myapp/config.yml ]]; then
  echo "config missing — aborting" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "config found, continuing"
exit 0
bash
`>&2` redirects the message to standard error, the proper channel for warnings.
Try it in the shell playground

Reading about scripts only takes you so far — the concepts stick once you watch them run. Open the shell scripting playground, create a file with the shebang, `chmod +x` it, and run it. Then deliberately break something: drop the quotes around a variable holding a space, or check `$?` after a command that fails. Seeing the failure mode firsthand is the fastest way to internalise why the safe habits matter.

title: Bash Variables, Conditionals, and Loops
summary: Control the flow of a script with tests, branches, and the three kinds of loops Bash gives you.
seo_title: Bash Variables, Conditionals, and Loops — Control Flow Explained
seo_description: Master Bash control flow: variables and parameter expansion, test conditions with [[ ]], if/elif/case, and for/while/until loops. Hands-on examples in a free sandbox.
seo_keywords: bash, variables, conditionals, if, case, for loop, while loop, arrays, parameter expansion
sections: Variables and the dollar of expansion

You assign a Bash variable with `name=value` and absolutely no spaces around the `=` — `name = value` is read as a command called `name`, not an assignment. You read the value back by prefixing the name with `$`, and you should almost always wrap that in double quotes and braces: `"${name}"`.

The braces are not just style. They mark exactly where the variable name ends, so `"${file}_backup"` works while `"$file_backup"` would (wrongly) look for a variable literally named `file_backup`. Get in the habit of `${...}` and a whole category of confusing bugs disappears.

service=nginx
port=8080

echo "Starting ${service} on port ${port}"

log="/var/log/${service}.log"   # braces disambiguate the name
echo "Logging to ${log}"
bash
No spaces around `=`; braces around the name when you expand it.
Defaults and parameter expansion

Bash can supply a fallback when a variable is unset or empty, which makes scripts resilient to missing input. The form `${VAR:-default}` evaluates to `default` only when `VAR` has no value, leaving `VAR` itself untouched. The cousin `${VAR:=default}` also assigns the default back into the variable.

Parameter expansion does much more than defaults — it can trim, slice, and replace text without calling out to external tools like `sed`. Two everyday forms: `${path##*/}` strips everything up to the last slash (the basename), and `${file%.txt}` removes a trailing `.txt` suffix.
bash
`$1` is the first argument passed to the script.
Testing conditions with [[ ]]

Conditionals start with a test. In Bash, prefer the `[[ ... ]]` keyword over the older `[ ... ]` command: it is safer with unquoted variables, supports `&&`/`||` inside it, and understands pattern matching. The test produces an exit status that `if` then branches on.

Learn a handful of operators and you can express most checks. For files: `-f` (regular file exists), `-d` (directory exists), `-e` (any kind exists), `-r`/`-w`/`-x` (readable/writable/executable). For strings: `-z` (empty), `-n` (non-empty), `==` and `!=`. For integers, use the word forms `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge`, because `<` and `>` inside `[[ ]]` compare alphabetically, not numerically.

file=/etc/hosts

if [[ -f "$file" && -r "$file" ]]; then
  echo "$file exists and is readable"
fi

count=5
if [[ "$count" -gt 3 ]]; then
  echo "count ($count) is greater than three"
fi

name="web-01"
if [[ "$name" == web-* ]]; then    # glob pattern match
  echo "$name is a web host"
fi
bash
Use -gt/-lt for numbers; == with a glob does pattern matching.
Branching with if/elif and case

An `if`/`elif`/`else` chain handles a small number of distinct conditions, evaluated top to bottom until one matches. It is the right tool when each branch tests something different.

When you are matching one value against many possible patterns, `case` is far cleaner than a tower of `elif`s. Each branch lists a pattern (globs allowed, `|` separates alternatives) ending in `)`, the commands to run, and a `;;` to close it. The `*)` branch at the end is the catch-all default.
bash
`read -rp` prints a prompt and reads the reply into $action.
Looping over lists with for

A `for` loop binds a variable to each item of a list in turn and runs the body once per item. The list can be literal words, the result of a glob, the output of a command, or a numeric range. This is the natural way to apply one action across many hosts, files, or steps.

A crucial subtlety: to loop over files, use a glob (`for f in *.log`) rather than the output of `ls`. Globbing handles filenames with spaces correctly and quietly skips the parsing problems that `for f in $(ls)` introduces. Bash also offers a C-style `for ((...))` when you genuinely need a counter.

# Iterate a literal list
for host in web-01 web-02 db-01; do
  echo "Pinging ${host}"
done

# Iterate files safely with a glob
for logfile in /var/log/*.log; do
  echo "Found ${logfile} ($(wc -l < "$logfile") lines)"
done

# C-style counter loop
for (( i = 1; i <= 3; i++ )); do
  echo "attempt ${i}"
done
bash
Glob over files instead of parsing `ls` to stay safe with odd names.
while, until, and reading input line by line

A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition stays true; `until` is its mirror image, repeating until the condition *becomes* true. Both are handy for polling, retrying, and consuming a stream.

The single most useful `while` pattern is reading a file or command output one line at a time.
