title: PostgreSQL Indexes and EXPLAIN: Making Slow Queries Fast
summary: Understand how indexes work, read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, and decide when an index will (and will not) help.
seo_title: PostgreSQL Indexes and EXPLAIN ANALYZE Explained
seo_description: Learn how PostgreSQL indexes work, how to read EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and when an index speeds up or slows down a query. Hands-on SQL examples included.
seo_keywords: postgresql, index, explain, explain analyze, b-tree, seq scan, index scan, query performance, composite index
sections: The problem an index solves

Imagine a table with a million orders and a query that asks for the orders belonging to one customer. With no index, PostgreSQL has only one option: read every row, check each one, and discard the millions it does not want. This is a sequential scan, and its cost grows with the size of the whole table even though you only wanted a handful of rows.

An index is a separate, sorted data structure that lets PostgreSQL jump straight to the matching rows instead of reading everything. The analogy is the index at the back of a book: rather than skim every page looking for a term, you look it up alphabetically and the index tells you exactly which pages to turn to. The trade-off is the same too: the index takes extra space, and every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must also update the index, so writes get slightly slower.

PostgreSQL's default and most useful index type is the B-tree, which keeps keys sorted and balanced. It is the right choice for equality (=), ranges (<, >, BETWEEN), and ORDER BY on the indexed column. The rest of this tutorial uses B-tree indexes unless noted.

-- our working table for this tutorial
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          serial PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL,
  status      text    NOT NULL,
  amount_cents integer NOT NULL,
  placed_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
sql
PRIMARY KEY already creates a B-tree index on id automatically.
Reading EXPLAIN: the plan before you optimise

Never guess at performance. PostgreSQL will tell you exactly how it intends to run a query if you prefix it with EXPLAIN. The output is the query plan: a tree of steps, read from the most-indented inner node outward. EXPLAIN alone only estimates; it does not run the query, so it is safe and instant.

The two lines you will care about most are the scan type and the cost numbers. 'Seq Scan' means PostgreSQL plans to read the whole table. The cost is shown as cost=start..total in arbitrary planner units, alongside the estimated row count. These are estimates derived from table statistics, not real timings, but they tell you which strategy the planner chose and roughly how expensive it thinks each step is.

EXPLAIN
SELECT id, amount_cents
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Typical output on an un-indexed table:
--  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=12 width=8)
--    Filter: (customer_id = 42)
sql
Seq Scan + a Filter line is the classic signature of a missing index.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE: measuring what really happens

EXPLAIN ANALYZE goes further: it actually executes the query and reports real timings and real row counts next to the estimates. This is the tool you reach for when you are tuning, because it exposes two things plain EXPLAIN cannot: the actual milliseconds spent, and any gap between estimated and actual rows.

That estimate-versus-actual gap is gold. If the planner expected 12 rows but 80,000 came back, its statistics are stale or skewed, and it may have picked a bad plan as a result. Because EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query, never run it casually against an UPDATE or DELETE in production unless you wrap it in a transaction you intend to roll back. For SELECTs it is completely safe.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, amount_cents
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42;

--  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=12 width=8)
--                       (actual time=0.41..142.6 rows=11 loops=1)
--    Filter: (customer_id = 42)
--    Rows Removed by Filter: 999989
--  Planning Time: 0.18 ms
--  Execution Time: 143.0 ms
sql
'Rows Removed by Filter: 999989' is the wasted work an index would eliminate.
Creating an index and watching the plan change

Now create a B-tree index on the column we filter by and run the same EXPLAIN ANALYZE again. The scan type should flip from Seq Scan to Index Scan (or Bitmap Index Scan for less selective queries), and the execution time should drop sharply because PostgreSQL stops touching the 999,989 rows it does not want.

A crucial habit: after a large data change or a fresh index on an existing table, run ANALYZE so the planner refreshes its statistics. Without current statistics the planner can keep choosing the old plan because it does not yet know the index is worthwhile. Index creation does collect some statistics, but ANALYZE makes them reliable.
sql
143 ms to 0.11 ms: the Index Cond replaced the full-table Filter.
Composite indexes and why column order matters

When a query filters on more than one column, a multi-column (composite) index can cover the whole condition. But column order in the index is not arbitrary. A B-tree on (customer_id, status) is sorted by customer_id first and only by status within each customer. So this index helps queries that filter on customer_id alone, or on customer_id AND status, but it does not help a query that filters on status alone, because status is scattered all through the index.

The practical rule of thumb: put the column used for equality first, and the column used for ranges or sorting later. An index on (customer_id, placed_at) is excellent for 'this customer's orders, newest first', because PostgreSQL can seek to the customer and then walk the already-sorted dates without a separate sort step.
sql
A composite index is usable left-to-right; the leading column is mandatory.
When indexes do not help (or actively hurt)

Indexes are not free magic, and several common situations defeat them. The first is low selectivity: if a query matches a large fraction of the table (say status = 'paid' when most orders are paid), PostgreSQL may correctly decide a sequential scan is cheaper than bouncing in and out of an index thousands of times. A faithful EXPLAIN showing a Seq Scan here is the planner being smart, not broken.

The second is wrapping the indexed column in a function or expression. WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com' cannot use a plain index on email, because the index stores email, not lower(email). The fix is an expression index built on lower(email). The third is leading wildcards: LIKE '%smith' cannot use a normal B-tree because the index is sorted from the front of the string. Finally, every index slows writes and consumes disk, so do not index columns you never filter or sort on.
sql
Match the index to the exact expression the query uses.
A repeatable tuning workflow

Put it together into a loop you can run on any slow query. First, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and identify the most expensive node and any Seq Scan over a large table with a tight filter. Second, check the estimate-versus-actual row counts; a big gap means you should ANALYZE the table to refresh statistics before doing anything else. Third, add the narrowest index that matches the query's WHERE and ORDER BY, mind the leading-column rule, and re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm the plan actually changed and the time dropped.

Resist the urge to add indexes speculatively. Each one is a standing cost on every write and a chunk of disk. The discipline is: measure, add one targeted index, measure again, and keep it only if EXPLAIN ANALYZE proves it earned its place.
sql
Open the SQL playground, seed a wide table, and watch Seq Scan become Index Scan.

title: Transactions and ACID in PostgreSQL: Keeping Data Correct
summary: Master BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, the ACID guarantees, isolation levels, and how to avoid lost updates and deadlocks.
seo_title: PostgreSQL Transactions and ACID: Isolation Levels and Locking
seo_description: A deep, practical guide to PostgreSQL transactions: ACID, BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, isolation levels, lost updates, SELECT FOR UPDATE, and avoiding deadlocks.
seo_keywords: postgresql, transactions, acid, isolation level, serializable, repeatable read, select for update, deadlock, mvcc, savepoint
sections: What a transaction is and why you need one

A transaction groups several statements into a single all-or-nothing unit of work. The textbook example is a money transfer: subtract from one account, add to another. If the database crashes (or a constraint fails) after the first step but before the second, you must never end up with money deducted from one side and never credited to the other. A transaction guarantees that either both steps happen or neither does.

In PostgreSQL you open a transaction with BEGIN, make your changes, and finish with COMMIT to make them permanent or ROLLBACK to discard everything since the BEGIN. Until you commit, your changes are invisible to other sessions and fully reversible. Notably, in PostgreSQL even schema changes like CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE are transactional, so a failed migration can be cleanly rolled back, which is not true of every database.
sql
Without BEGIN, each statement auto-commits on its own and cannot be undone.
The four ACID guarantees, concretely

ACID is the set of promises a transaction makes. Atomicity is the all-or-nothing rule from the transfer above: the transaction is indivisible, so partial application is impossible. Consistency means a committed transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting every constraint, foreign key, and check you defined; a transaction that would violate them is rejected, not partially applied.

Isolation means concurrent transactions do not step on each other; each behaves, within limits set by its isolation level, as though it were running alone. Durability means once COMMIT returns success, the data survives a crash or power loss, because PostgreSQL has flushed the change to its write-ahead log (WAL) on disk before acknowledging. The next sections drill into isolation, because it is the one with knobs you can turn and the one most likely to surprise you.
sql
A CHECK constraint makes 'never negative' a guarantee, not a hope.
MVCC: how PostgreSQL gives readers a stable view

Under the hood PostgreSQL uses Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC). Instead of locking rows for readers, it keeps multiple versions of a row and shows each transaction the version appropriate to when its snapshot was taken. The headline consequence is liberating: readers never block writers and writers never block readers. A long-running report does not freeze out the application updating the same tables.

MVCC is why your transaction can see a consistent snapshot even while others are committing changes around you. The cost is that obsolete row versions (dead tuples) accumulate and must be cleaned up by the autovacuum process; this is normal background housekeeping. The behavioural details, like whether you see other sessions' committed changes mid-transaction, are governed by your isolation level.
sql
What a re-read shows depends entirely on the isolation level.
Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent

SQL defines three anomalies that concurrent transactions can suffer. A dirty read sees another transaction's uncommitted changes; PostgreSQL never allows this, so its lowest level already behaves like READ COMMITTED. A non-repeatable read happens when you read a row twice and get different committed values because someone changed it in between. A phantom read happens when you run the same filtered query twice and a new matching row has appeared.

PostgreSQL offers three usable levels. READ COMMITTED (the default) sees each statement's own fresh snapshot, so it can show non-repeatable and phantom reads. REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot at the start of the transaction and holds it, eliminating both non-repeatable and phantom reads. SERIALIZABLE is the strictest: it guarantees the outcome is equivalent to running the transactions one after another, and it will abort a transaction with a serialization error if that guarantee would be violated, leaving you to retry.
sql
Set the level right after BEGIN, before the first query.
The lost update problem and SELECT FOR UPDATE

Here is the classic concurrency bug. Two sessions both read a counter as 10, both add 1 in application code, and both write back 11. One increment vanished: that is a lost update. Read-modify-write cycles in application logic are where this bites hardest, and a plain SELECT followed by an UPDATE in separate steps is wide open to it.

There are two clean fixes. The simplest is to do the arithmetic inside the database with a single UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1, which is atomic and immune to the race. When you genuinely must read a value, decide something in your code, and then write it back, lock the row on the way in with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. That acquires a row lock so any other session trying to lock or update the same row waits until you commit, serialising the dangerous section.
sql
FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
Savepoints: partial rollback inside a transaction

Sometimes you want most of a transaction to succeed but need a do-over on one risky step without throwing away everything. SAVEPOINT marks a point you can roll back to with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT, leaving the work before the savepoint intact and the transaction still open. This is how you attempt an operation that might fail, and recover gracefully if it does.

Savepoints matter for another PostgreSQL-specific reason: once any statement in a transaction raises an error, the whole transaction is poisoned and every subsequent statement fails with 'current transaction is aborted' until you roll back. Wrapping a fallible statement between a savepoint and a release lets you catch its failure, roll back just that statement, and carry on with the rest of the transaction.
sql
ROLLBACK TO rewinds to the savepoint; the transaction stays open.
Deadlocks: why they happen and how to avoid them

A deadlock is a standoff: transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and wants row 2, while transaction B holds row 2 and wants row 1. Neither can proceed. PostgreSQL detects the cycle automatically, picks one transaction as the victim, and aborts it with a deadlock error so the other can finish. Your application should catch that error and retry the aborted transaction.

The most effective prevention is a convention, not a feature: always acquire locks in a consistent order. If every transaction that touches multiple accounts locks them in ascending id order, the circular wait can never form. Keep transactions short so locks are held briefly, do the minimum work between BEGIN and COMMIT, and never leave a transaction open while waiting on slow external work like a network call or user input.
sql
Consistent lock ordering is the simplest deadlock cure.
Practise transactions safely in the SQL console

Transactions are best understood by breaking them on purpose where it costs nothing. Open the free PostgreSQL console playground and build the accounts table with a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint. Then deliberately trigger each behaviour: start a transfer, ROLLBACK, and confirm the balances are untouched. Force the CHECK to fail and watch the whole transaction abort atomically. Use a SAVEPOINT to recover from one bad statement while keeping the rest.

The habits to carry into real systems are small but decisive: keep transactions short, prefer atomic UPDATE ... SET col = col + n over read-then-write, reach for SELECT FOR UPDATE when you truly must read-decide-write, raise the isolation level only when correctness demands it, and lock rows in a consistent order to keep deadlocks out. Get these into your fingers here, where a mistake is just a ROLLBACK away.
sql
Seed this in the playground, then experiment with COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT.

title: Python Data Structures: Lists, Dictionaries, and Sets
summary: Choose the right built-in container — ordered lists, key/value dicts, and uniqueness-enforcing sets — and use them well.
seo_title: Python Data Structures: Lists, Dictionaries, and Sets Explained
seo_description: A hands-on guide to Python's core containers — lists, dictionaries, and sets — when to use each, and the operations you'll reach for daily. Try every example live.
seo_keywords: python, data structures, lists, dictionaries, dict, sets, collections, beginner, tutorial
sections: Three containers, three jobs

Most everyday Python work comes down to moving data in and out of three built-in containers: the list, the dictionary, and the set. They look superficially similar — they all hold a bunch of values — but each is tuned for a different question. A list answers "what is the order of these things?" A dictionary answers "what value is associated with this key?" A set answers "is this thing in the group, and is it unique?"

Picking the right one is the difference between code that reads clearly and runs fast, and code that loops where it shouldn't. This tutorial walks through all three with examples you can paste straight into a Python prompt.
Lists keep things in order

A list is an ordered, changeable sequence written with square brackets. Items keep the position you put them in, you reach any item by its index (counting from zero), and a list happily holds duplicates and mixed types. This is the container to reach for when sequence matters — a queue of tasks, rows read from a file, the steps of a recipe.

Negative indexes count from the end, which is a tidy way to grab the last item without first asking how long the list is.

tasks = ["backup", "deploy", "verify"]
print(tasks[0])        # first item  -> backup
print(tasks[-1])       # last item   -> verify

tasks.append("notify")   # add to the end
tasks.insert(0, "plan")  # add at the front
print(tasks)             # ['plan', 'backup', 'deploy', 'verify', 'notify']
python
Indexing is zero-based; tasks[-1] is the same as tasks[len(tasks) - 1].
Slicing and editing lists

Beyond single items, a slice pulls out a whole range with the `start:stop` syntax — the start is included, the stop is not. Slices are forgiving: asking for more than exists simply returns what's there rather than raising an error.

Because lists are mutable you can change them in place. Assigning to an index overwrites one item, `remove` deletes by value, and `pop` removes by position and hands the value back to you so you can use it.

nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:3])      # [20, 30]  (stop index excluded)
print(nums[:2])       # [10, 20] (from the start)
print(nums[3:])       # [40, 50] (to the end)

nums[0] = 99          # overwrite the first item
nums.remove(30)       # delete the value 30
last = nums.pop()     # remove and return the final item
print(nums, "popped", last)
python
A slice never changes the original list — it returns a new one.
Dictionaries map keys to values

A dictionary stores pairs: each unique key points at a value. Written with curly braces and colons, it is the right tool whenever you want to look something up by name rather than by position — a user's settings, a count per category, a row addressed by its id.

Lookups are fast no matter how big the dictionary grows, because Python hashes the key rather than scanning. Reach for a value with square brackets when you're sure the key exists, or with `.get()` when it might not, supplying a fallback so a missing key doesn't crash your program.

user = {"name": "Ada", "role": "admin", "active": True}
print(user["name"])              # Ada
print(user.get("email", "n/a"))  # key missing -> 'n/a'

user["email"] = "ada@example.com"  # add a new pair
user["role"] = "owner"              # overwrite an existing one
print(user)
python
user["missing"] raises KeyError; user.get("missing") returns None instead.
Looping over a dictionary

Most dictionary work happens in a loop. Iterating the dictionary directly gives you the keys; pair it with `.items()` to unpack both the key and value at once, which is almost always what you want when reporting or transforming data.

A common pattern is counting: start each key at zero (or use `.get(key, 0)`), then add to it as you encounter items. This turns a flat list into a tally without any nested loops.
python
.get(choice, 0) returns 0 the first time a choice is seen, avoiding a KeyError.
Sets enforce uniqueness

A set is an unordered collection that automatically discards duplicates. The instant you need "the distinct values" or "have I seen this before?", a set is the answer. Build one with curly braces (or the `set()` constructor for an empty one — `{}` makes an empty dictionary, a classic gotcha).

Membership testing with `in` is fast on a set, the same way key lookup is fast on a dictionary, so checking thousands of values against a set beats checking them against a list.
python
Passing a list to set() is the one-liner for de-duplicating it.
Set math: union, intersection, difference

Sets really shine when you compare two groups. The operators read like the maths they implement: `|` is union (everything in either), `&` is intersection (only what's in both), and `-` is difference (in the first but not the second). These replace fiddly nested loops with a single, obvious line.

A practical example: given the permissions a user has and the permissions an action requires, intersection tells you what they're allowed to do and difference tells you what they're still missing.
python
issubset answers 'does the user have only valid permissions?' in one call.
Choosing the right one

When you finish a snippet, ask what question it really answers. Need to preserve order or keep duplicates? Use a list. Looking things up by a name or id? Use a dictionary. Care only about membership and uniqueness? Use a set. Many bugs and slow loops disappear the moment the data lives in the right container.

The fastest way to internalise the differences is to run the examples and poke at them. Open the Python playground, paste each block, then change a value and predict the output before you press run.

title: Python Functions and Comprehensions
summary: Write expressive functions with default and keyword arguments, then compress loops into readable comprehensions.
seo_title: Python Functions and Comprehensions — Arguments, *args, lambdas, and List Comprehensions
seo_description: Level up your Python: default and keyword arguments, *args/**kwargs, lambdas, and list/dict/set comprehensions, with runnable examples in a free online compiler.
seo_keywords: python, functions, arguments, kwargs, args, lambda, list comprehension, dict comprehension, intermediate
sections: From calling functions to designing them

Once you can call `len()` and `print()`, the next step is designing your own functions well. A good function does one thing, has a name that says what that thing is, and accepts its inputs in a way callers find natural. Get the signature right and the rest of your code reads like prose.

This tutorial assumes you've met `def` and `return` and pushes into the parts that make functions pleasant to use: flexible arguments, small anonymous functions, and the comprehension syntax that lets a whole loop collapse into one clear line.

def area(width, height):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))   # 12
python
A docstring (the triple-quoted line) documents what the function does.
Default and keyword arguments

Default values let a function be called simply in the common case yet stay configurable when needed. List the parameter with an `=` and a fallback; callers who omit it get the default. Callers can also pass arguments by name, which makes a call site self-documenting — you read `retries=3` and instantly know what the 3 means.

One firm rule: never use a mutable value like a list or dict as a default. That single object is shared across every call, so it accumulates state between calls in surprising ways. Use `None` as the default and create a fresh object inside the function instead.

def connect(host, port=5432, timeout=30):
    print(f"connecting to {host}:{port} (timeout {timeout}s)")

connect("db-01")                    # uses both defaults
connect("db-01", timeout=5)         # override just one, by name
connect("db-01", port=6432, timeout=5)

# Safe pattern for a mutable default:
def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    tags = tags or []
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags
python
Keyword arguments can be given in any order, unlike positional ones.
Accepting any number of arguments

Sometimes you don't know in advance how many values a caller will pass. `*args` gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple, and `**kwargs` gathers extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. Together they let a function be wonderfully flexible — this is exactly how helpers like `print()` accept any number of items.

The same star syntax works in reverse at the call site: a `*` in front of a list unpacks it into positional arguments, and `**` unpacks a dict into keyword arguments. That symmetry is worth remembering — the stars mean "spread these out" in both directions.

def summarize(label, *values, **options):
    sep = options.get("sep", ", ")
    print(f"{label}: {sep.join(str(v) for v in values)}")

summarize("scores", 90, 85, 77)
summarize("hosts", "a", "b", sep=" | ")

nums = [1, 2, 3]
summarize("unpacked", *nums)   # the * spreads the list into args
python
args is a tuple, kwargs is a dict — inspect them with print() to see.
Returning more than one value

Python functions can hand back several values at once by returning them comma-separated, which packs them into a tuple. The caller then unpacks that tuple into separate names in a single line. This is cleaner than returning a list and indexing into it, because each returned thing gets a real name.

If a caller only cares about some of the results, the underscore `_` is the conventional name for "a value I'm deliberately ignoring."

def divmod_pair(a, b):
    quotient = a // b
    remainder = a % b
    return quotient, remainder   # returns a tuple

q, r = divmod_pair(17, 5)
print(q, r)        # 3 2

_, leftover = divmod_pair(17, 5)   # ignore the quotient
print(leftover)    # 2
python
q, r = ... is tuple unpacking — the comma on the left does the work.
Small functions on the fly: lambda

A `lambda` is a tiny, unnamed function written in a single expression. You'd never write a big lambda — that's what `def` is for — but they're perfect as a throwaway argument to functions that take other functions, most commonly the `key` parameter of `sorted`.

The `key` function is called once per item and returns the value to sort by. A lambda lets you express "sort by the second element" or "sort by length" right where you need it, without defining a named helper you'll never reuse.

people = [("Ada", 36), ("Linus", 54), ("Grace", 85)]

by_age = sorted(people, key=lambda person: person[1])
print(by_age)   # [('Ada', 36), ('Linus', 54), ('Grace', 85)]

words = ["pip", "python", "go"]
by_length = sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w))
print(by_length)   # ['go', 'pip', 'python']
python
lambda person: person[1] is a one-line function taking person, returning person[1].
List comprehensions

A list comprehension builds a new list from an existing iterable in one expression. Read it as "the expression, for each item, in the source" — it does exactly what a `for` loop with `append` does, but in a single readable line that signals "I am producing a list."

You can add a trailing `if` to keep only the items you want. The result is code that states the *what* ("squares of the even numbers") rather than the mechanical *how* of looping and appending.

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

squares = [n * n for n in nums]
print(squares)   # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36]

even_squares = [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(even_squares)   # [4, 16, 36]

# Equivalent verbose form, for comparison:
out = []
for n in nums:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        out.append(n * n)
python
Keep comprehensions short; if one needs two lines of logic, use a loop.
Dict and set comprehensions

The same bracket-free syntax works for dictionaries and sets — just change the brackets and, for a dict, supply a `key: value` pair. A dict comprehension is the idiomatic way to build a lookup table from a sequence, and a set comprehension produces distinct results in one step.

A frequent real-world use is inverting or re-keying data: turn a list of records into a dictionary indexed by id, or build a set of the unique categories present, all without an explicit loop.
python
Curly braces with a colon make a dict; without a colon, a set.
Putting it together

Flexible arguments and comprehensions are the two habits that most distinguish tidy intermediate Python from a beginner's. A well-named function with sensible defaults is a joy to call, and a comprehension turns a five-line loop into one line that states intent.

The catch is that both can be over-applied — a function with ten arguments or a triple-nested comprehension is harder to read than the loop it replaced. Aim for clarity first. Open the Python playground, run each example, and try rewriting one of your own loops as a comprehension to feel where the line is.

summary: Read and write files safely, handle errors with try/except, and structure code into reusable modules and packages.

seo_description: Read and write files with context managers, handle errors with try/except/finally, raise your own exceptions, and split code into modules and packages. Runnable examples included.
seo_keywords: python, files, file io, with statement, exceptions, try except, error handling, modules, packages, import, advanced
sections: Programs that touch the real world

The moment your code reads a file, calls an API, or parses user input, it has to cope with things going wrong: the file is missing, the data is malformed, the disk is full. Robust programs don't pretend failure can't happen — they anticipate it and respond deliberately.

This tutorial covers the three pillars of dependable Python: reading and writing files correctly, handling errors with exceptions, and organising code into modules so a growing program stays navigable. These are the skills that separate a script that works on your machine from one others can rely on.
Reading files with a context manager

Open a file with `open()`, but always inside a `with` block. The `with` statement is a context manager: it guarantees the file is closed for you when the block ends, even if an error is raised partway through. Forgetting to close files is a classic source of leaks and locked-file bugs, and `with` makes that impossible to forget.

The mode string controls intent: `"r"` reads (the default), `"w"` writes a fresh file, and `"a"` appends. For text, also pass `encoding="utf-8"` so your code behaves the same on every platform rather than guessing the encoding.

with open("notes.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    content = f.read()          # whole file as one string
print(content)

# Line by line is memory-friendly for large files:
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.rstrip())     # rstrip() drops the trailing newline
python
After the with block the file is guaranteed closed — no f.close() needed.
Writing and appending

Writing uses the same `with` pattern with a different mode. Be careful: opening in `"w"` mode truncates the file to empty the instant it opens, so an existing file's contents are gone before you write a single byte. Use `"a"` when you mean to add to what's already there, such as a log.

The `write()` method does not add newlines for you — you control them — which is occasionally surprising the first time. For writing many lines, `writelines()` or a loop with explicit `"\n"` both work cleanly.

lines = ["first run ok", "second run ok"]

with open("run.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in lines:
        f.write(line + "\n")     # write() adds no newline itself

with open("run.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("third run ok\n")     # append, keeping earlier lines

print(open("run.log", encoding="utf-8").read())
python
Mode 'w' wipes the file on open; 'a' preserves it and adds to the end.
Catching errors with try/except

An exception is Python's way of signalling that something went wrong. Left unhandled it stops the program with a traceback. Wrap the risky operation in a `try` block and catch the specific exception you expect in an `except` block, so your program can recover or report cleanly instead of crashing.

Catch the narrowest exception type that fits — `FileNotFoundError`, `ValueError`, `KeyError` — rather than a bare `except:` that swallows everything, including the bugs you actually want to see. Naming the exception with `as` gives you the message to log.
python
Each except handles one failure mode; unexpected errors still surface loudly.
else, finally, and clean-up

A `try` block can have two more parts. The `else` block runs only when no exception was raised — a good home for the "happy path" logic that should not itself be guarded by the `try`. The `finally` block runs no matter what, success or failure, which is where you put clean-up that must always happen, like releasing a lock or closing a network connection.

Keeping the `try` body small — just the one operation that can fail — and moving the follow-on work into `else` makes it crystal clear which line you expected to throw and which code only matters when it didn't.
python
finally always runs; else runs only when the try block succeeded.
Raising your own exceptions

Handling errors is only half the story — sometimes your code is the thing that detects a problem, and the right move is to `raise` an exception so the caller can decide what to do. Raising early, close to where a bad value is first seen, produces far clearer tracebacks than letting a corrupt value cause a mysterious failure ten functions later.

For domain-specific problems, define your own exception class by subclassing `Exception`. A descriptive name like `ConfigError` tells anyone reading a traceback exactly what category of thing failed, and lets callers catch that category specifically.
python
Subclassing Exception gives you a named error callers can target directly.
Splitting code into modules

Any `.py` file is a module, and `import` pulls its names into another file. Once a program outgrows a single file, splitting related functions into their own modules — `auth.py`, `storage.py`, `utils.py` — keeps each file focused and lets you reuse pieces across projects. Import a whole module and use dotted access, or import specific names directly.

The `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard is the key idiom here. Code under it runs only when the file is executed directly, not when it's imported. That lets a module offer functions for reuse *and* do something useful when run on its own, without the two purposes colliding.

# file: mathutils.py
def mean(values):
    return sum(values) / len(values)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # runs only when you execute `python mathutils.py`
    print("self-test:", mean([2, 4, 6]))

# file: report.py
import mathutils
from mathutils import mean

print(mathutils.mean([10, 20]))   # dotted access
print(mean([10, 20]))             # imported name directly
python
The __main__ guard separates 'imported as a library' from 'run as a script'.
Packages: directories of modules

When you have several related modules, group them into a package — a directory of `.py` files. Modern Python treats any such directory as a package, though adding an `__init__.py` lets you control what the package exposes and run set-up code on import. You then import with dotted paths that mirror the folder layout.

The standard library is itself a vast collection of packages and modules — `json`, `pathlib`, `datetime`, `os` — and learning to reach for them first, before writing your own, is a hallmark of effective Python. The same `import` you use for your code pulls in those batteries-included tools.

# Directory layout:
#   myapp/
#     __init__.py
#     storage.py        # defines save()
#     auth.py           # defines login()

from myapp.storage import save
from myapp import auth

# Standard-library modules import exactly the same way:
import json
from pathlib import Path

config = json.loads('{"port": 5432}')
print(Path("run.log").exists())
python
Dotted import paths (myapp.storage) mirror the directory structure on disk.
Build something resilient

You now have the toolkit for code that survives contact with the real world: files opened and closed safely with `with`, failures caught precisely with `try`/`except`/`finally`, your own exceptions raised where problems start, and a project split into modules and packages that stay readable as it grows.

The best way to cement this is to write a small program that reads a file, validates its contents, and reports problems gracefully instead of crashing. Open the Python playground, paste these snippets, and deliberately feed them bad input — a missing file, a non-numeric value — to watch your error handling do its job.
